item.title: [New York Daily News] Key dates & storylines as Mets approach offseason
item.dc:creator: Abbey Mastracco

item.content:encoded:
When the World Series concludes, the Mets can start to get a move on in their offseason.
In what is expected to be a turbulent winter, the Mets don’t have an immense amount of business to take care of before the expected lockout on Dec. 1. They traded away the veterans who were on expiring contracts at the deadline over the summer and installed a manager, Andy Green, before the end of the regular season. The club is looking to make some minor changes to the coaching staff after firing hitting coach Jeff Albert, and in the front office, where the team is seeking a farm director to replace Green.
Here are key dates and storylines to watch for as the offseason approaches.
DAY AFTER THE WORLD SERIES: FREE AGENCY
After the commissioner’s trophy is awarded, a five-day “quiet period” begins where pending free agents can negotiate with their current teams. Bo Bichette is the only potential free agent for the Mets. The third baseman has a player option for 2027 and one for 2028, and will have five days from the conclusion of the World Series to make a decision.
Late in the season, Bichette sounded as though he was leaning toward staying in Queens, but nothing is final.
It was an uncharacteristic season for the infielder. He played third base for the first time, though he was moved back to his natural shortstop position for a few months while Francisco Lindor was on the injured list. He hit just .260, though he matched his 2025 home run total with 18.
Bichette, 28, often lamented his inability to come through for the team in the first half, saying if he had, the Mets might have been in a better position. A good teammate with a strong work ethic, the Mets want him back. With the lockout looming, it might benefit him to take the option for next season instead of trying to feel out free agency for the second year in a row.
Free agents can negotiate with other teams after the quiet period ends. The biggest name on the market is Los Angeles Dodgers ace and two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. The Mets, in need of starting pitching, should do what they can to sign the lefty.
NOV. 10-12: GENERAL MANAGER MEETINGS
The GM Meetings used to be a quiet affair. Rule changes were discussed at resorts around various Southwestern cities. It’s where executives used to lay the framework for roster building, discussing things in broad terms and doing initial check-ins on items they would later circle back to at the Winter Meetings.
That isn’t the case this season. The meetings have moved to Las Vegas for the foreseeable future, a city that is anything but quiet, and they now precede the MLB Awards Show, a full-blown red-carpet affair. The Winter Meetings will be canceled if the league locks out the players, so teams are expected to meet with players in Las Vegas instead of waiting until December.
NOV. 17: DEADLINE TO ACCEPT QUALIFYING OFFERS
Eligible players have until 4 p.m. ET to accept or reject the qualifying offer.
NOV. 20: NON-TENDER DEADLINE
The final date for teams to offer a contract to all arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players on their 40-man roster for next season; this is where the Mets have some tough decisions to make. Their list of arbitration-eligible players is long: Mark Vientos, Brett Baty, Francisco Alvarez, Ronny Mauricio, Tylor Megill, Reed Garrett, Robert Stock and Austin Warren.
Vientos, Baty, Alvarez and Mauricio were once top prospects in the Mets’ system, but they aren’t prospects anymore.
Alvarez, a power-hitting catcher, was primarily the Mets’ full-time catcher until this season, when his defense was so poor the team had to use Luis Torrens as the main backstop. Injuries are also a concern for Alvarez, who has spent significant time on the injured list in each of the last three seasons. But he’s a well-liked, well-respected catcher, and it’s tough to let someone with his power go.
Though it’s clear the pop is still there, Vientos doesn’t have a full-time position, and he’s struggled as a platoon hitter over the last two seasons. The Mets converted Baty, a third baseman, to a super utility role this season, using him at first base and in the outfield in addition to second and third base. Though his outfield defense was particularly lacking, the Mets were happy with how he approached the season and the professionalism he showed in embracing a new challenge.
It’s tough to know what to do with Mauricio. The time he lost from his knee injury clearly stunted his development; he’s struggled to hit breaking balls at the big-league level, and he’s out of minor league options. But the switch-hitter can seriously impact the baseball and play multiple infield positions. Veteran infielders Lindor and Marcus Semien both spent time on the IL last season, and they aren’t getting any younger, so keeping him around next season might be beneficial.
DEC. 1: EXPIRATION OF THE CBA
For the second time in five years, the 30 club owners are expected to lock out their players. All activity involving players on 40-man rosters will halt. Players and teams cannot communicate until a new CBA is agreed upon and ratified.

item.title: [CubsHQ] Seiya Suzuki projected to land massive $120 million contract
item.dc:creator: Tony Crumpton
item.description: Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki could be in line for a massive payday this offseason, with at least one team already generating buzz as a potential landing spot. item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs outfielder Seiya Suzuki could be in line for a massive payday this offseason, with at least one team already generating buzz as a potential landing spot.
Jim Bowden of The Athletic ranks Suzuki as the No. 6 overall free agent in his latest rankings and projects the 32-year-old outfielder to land a five-year, $120 million contract, averaging $24 million per season.
Suzuki is coming off the best season of his MLB career, batting .270 with 26 home runs, 86 RBIs and a .368 on-base percentage. He also posted a .473 slugging percentage, an .841 OPS and a 131 OPS+ while producing 5.1 WAR, according to Baseball-Reference.
While Suzuki has always been a productive offensive player, his improved defense in right field helped make 2026 his most complete season since arriving from Japan.
Rumors are growing that the Toronto Blue Jays will make Suzuki a priority this offseason as they look to strengthen their outfield and add lineup protection for superstar Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
Bowden lists Toronto and the Philadelphia Phillies as the two best potential landing spots for Suzuki.
The veteran outfielder has been one of Chicago's most consistent hitters since signing his original five-year, $85 million contract ahead of the 2022 season. Over his five seasons with the Cubs, Suzuki averaged more than 20 home runs per year and posted an OPS+ of at least 125 in each of the past four seasons.
His combination of offensive consistency, improved defense and experience makes him one of the more attractive position players available in free agency.
Bowden compared Suzuki's potential contract to several notable outfield deals, including Teoscar Hernández's three-year, $66 million agreement, Jung Hoo Lee's six-year, $113 million contract and Nick Castellanos' five-year, $100 million deal.
For the Cubs, Suzuki's projected price tag presents another difficult offseason decision.
Chicago already faces significant uncertainty in its outfield, with several players potentially departing through free agency. Losing Suzuki would create another hole in a lineup that ranked among baseball's most productive offenses in 2026.
At $24 million annually, bringing Suzuki back would require a big financial commitment from the Cubs, who also need to address their starting rotation and several other roster needs.

item.content:encoded:
Outfielder and team captain Christian Yelich summed things up following the Milwaukee Brewers' heartbreaking, 4-3 loss in extra innings to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday.
Speaking to reporters after the Brewers allowed a golden opportunity to close out the series to slip through their fingers, Yelich said, "This stuff is not supposed to be easy. It's supposed to test you."
Trailing by scores of 1-0 and 2-1, the Brewers twice battled back to tie things up in Game 4 thanks to an RBI double by Cooper Pratt and solo home run by David Hamilton.
That allowed Milwaukee to force extra innings, and after the teams failed to score in the 10th and 11th innings, Pratt smacked a solo homer in the top of the 12th to put the Brewers ahead 3-2.
Milwaukee entered the bottom of the 12th needing three outs to win the first World Series in franchise history, but things went awry from there.
After Junior Caminero began the inning by reaching first base on a throwing error by Joey Ortiz, Shane Drohan entered the game and allowed four consecutive singles.
An RBI single by Jonny DeLuca tied it, and a walk-off RBI single by Ben Williamson won it, thus giving the Rays new life.
The Brewers still have a huge advantage, up 3-2 with likely National League Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski set to take the mound in Game 5 on Wednesday, but it is fair to wonder if losing Game 4 in such dramatic fashion could potentially mess with the Brew Crew's psyche.

item.title: [CubsHQ] Pete Crow-Armstrong sweeps two major MLB Players Choice Awards
item.dc:creator: Tony Crumpton
item.description: Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong continues to add to his impressive awards after a historic 2026 season. The Major League Baseball Players Association announced Wednesday that Crow-Armstrong has won both the 2026 Players Choice Awards Player of the Year and National League Outstanding Player honors. item.content:encoded:
Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong continues to add to his impressive awards after a historic 2026 season.
The Major League Baseball Players Association announced Wednesday that Crow-Armstrong has won both the 2026 Players Choice Awards Player of the Year and National League Outstanding Player honors.
Unlike awards voted on by baseball writers, the Players Choice Awards are determined exclusively by active MLB players, making the recognition even more meaningful for the 24-year-old Cubs star.
Crow-Armstrong put together one of the greatest individual seasons in franchise history, batting .280 with 45 home runs, 107 RBIs, 119 runs scored and 41 stolen bases. He also posted a .372 on-base percentage, .570 slugging percentage and .942 OPS while appearing in all 162 games.
His 45 home runs tied Philadelphia Phillies slugger Kyle Schwarber for the major league lead, while his 41 stolen bases made him just the seventh player in MLB history to record at least 40 home runs and 40 stolen bases in the same season. He also became the first Cubs player to accomplish the feat.
What makes Crow-Armstrong's season even more remarkable is his ability to impact games on both sides of the ball.
According to the MLBPA, Crow-Armstrong became the first player since Hall of Famer Cal Ripken Jr. in 1991 to finish among FanGraphs' top three players in both offensive and defensive value.
His combination of power, speed and elite defense in center field helped establish him as one of baseball's most complete players.
Crow-Armstrong was selected over fellow Player of the Year finalists Shohei Ohtani and Yordan Alvarez. He also beat out Ohtani and Schwarber for the NL Outstanding Player honor.
The latest recognition adds to an already impressive offseason for Crow-Armstrong, who has also received Player of the Year honors from Baseball America and Baseball Digest.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Brewers turn to Jacob Misiorowski in 2nd attempt to end World Series

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — With some pent-up energy and a fearless attitude, the Tampa Bay Rays extended their season at least one more day and will play host to Game 5 of the World Series on Wednesday.
With the Rays down to their last three outs, Jonny DeLuca and Ben Williamson provided the heroics to alter the narrative after Tampa Bay had been stymied at every turn over the first three games by the Milwaukee Brewers.
After falling into a 3-0 series hole, the Rays will now try to lean into their new-found momentum, but first they need to come up with a pitching plan.
Tampa Bay right-hander Nick Martinez would have been the probable Game 5 starter, but he was needed to pitch two innings on Tuesday.
“We’re going to get together after this session and sit down and talk about pitching,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said after the victory. “Going to check who’s available. I’m going to guess most guys are going to say they’re capable of an inning or more given it’s Game 5 of the World Series, but nothing has been decided yet.”
The Brewers tied the Tuesday game 2-2 in the fifth inning on a home run from David Hamilton, and the score remained even until the 12th when Cooper Pratt hit a home run for Milwaukee.
Down 3-2, Tampa Bay caught a rare break when Brewers third baseman Joey Ortiz committed a throwing error on Junior Caminero’s grounder to open the bottom of the 12th. Liam Hicks singled before DeLuca delivered an RBI single to center to tie the game 3-all.
After a Chandler Simpson single loaded the bases with no outs, Williamson came on to pinch-hit and bounced a ball into right field to set off a Rays celebration on the infield.
“Cash just kind of turned around and said, ‘Get ready to hit,'” Williamson said. “Jokingly in my head, I was thinking, ‘Yeah, I’ve been ready to hit since the fourth or fifth inning.'”
The Brewers now have one more opportunity to clinch their first-ever World Series title on the road, then would play host to Games 6 and 7, if necessary.
“Nobody said any of this was going to be easy, but I think we have the right group to get a good night’s sleep, flush it and be ready to go (Wednesday),” said Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers, who is 2-for-17 with three walks in the series after winning the National League Championship Series MVP award.
While Tampa Bay scrambles to put together a pitching plan, Milwaukee will send NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski to the mound. The hard-throwing right-hander allowed one run over five innings to earn the win in Game 1.
In three starts and 13 1/3 innings this postseason, Misiorowski is 1-0 with a 2.70 ERA and 14 strikeouts, although he had just three against the Rays in the series opener.
“You can write it up and hope that they perform like the back of their baseball card, but that doesn’t always happen,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said after announcing Misiorowski as his starter. “You go with what you believe is the deal. I trust our guys. They put themselves in a position to win.”
While the Rays used seven pitchers to keep their season alive in Game 4, the Brewers went even deeper by using eight in an unsuccessful attempt to close out their first-ever World Series championship. Game 5 could come down to which bullpen bounces back best.
“You’re seeing two elite contact offenses where strikeouts are very tough to come by,” Cash said. “We weren’t knocking balls in the gap or knocking balls out of the ballpark. We pieced together a big (12th inning), maybe the most important inning of our season.”
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays and Seiya Suzuki have been paired as a match for months.
It's easy enough during a given MLB season to look at upcoming free agents from multiple rosters and figure out who might have openings and who might have money to spend.
The Blue Jays have basically aligned with Suzuki, the free agent outfielder from the Chicago Cubs, in every way.
They'd even have a chance for him to join his Japanese countryman, Kazuma Okamoto, who just had a solid debut season in Toronto.
Free agency hasn't officially arrived yet, but that hasn't stopped the rumor mills and speculation from continuing.
And the latest update for the Blue Jays and Suzuki continues to suggest that they could end up together.
Seiya Suzuki Blue Jays Update
The Athletic's Jim Bowden wrote on Tuesday that he sees the Blue Jays as one of the best fits for Suzuki in free agency.
Bowden notes the Philadelphia Phillies as the team Toronto could have to compete with, and it's worth adding that Bowden has the Phillies interested in Randy Arozarena, too, but not the Blue Jays. So if Philadelphia ended up with Arozarena, that could help the Blue Jays get Suzuki.
"There is a lot of scuttlebutt in the industry that the Blue Jays are going to be targeting him as they look to add more offense to their outfield and more protection in their lineup for Vladimir Guerrero Jr.," writes Bowden. "Suzuki was a consistent performer for the Cubs over the past five years, averaging over 20 homers per season and an OPS+ of at least 125 over the past four seasons."
After a season in which the Blue Jays missed the playoffs, they certainly won't want to go the entire offseason without making a splash. Suzuki would qualify, particularly in a weak free agent hitter market.
Given all the chatter, there's really no surprise that Bowden is linking Suzuki to the Blue Jays, too. They'll still have to close the deal at some point.
Seiya Suzuki Contract Projection
Bowden also provided a contract projection for Suzuki as part of his blurb. He predicts a five-year deal for $120 million, which would be $24 million per year.
"Suzuki is coming off the best year of his MLB career," Bowden writes. "He had a .270/.368/.473 slash line with 26 homers and a 131 OPS+. He not only ranked among the better hitters in batting run value, but he improved his defense in right to become an asset there as well."
In a better free agent class, Suzuki might fly under the radar. In this one, he's going to be one of the prized signings, and the Blue Jays sure seem to be hoping he can be theirs.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Blue Jays' Seiya Suzuki Update Says What Everyone Is Thinking appeared first on HEAVY.

Game 4 of the World Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays begins at 8:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, October 27, televised by FOX. The Brewers are favored with a 1.75x payout to win on PrizePicks.
The Milwaukee Brewers lead 3-0 in the World Series after routing the Tampa Bay Rays 10-1 in Game 3 on Monday. Milwaukee is now one win away from securing the franchise's first World Series championship, while Tampa Bay faces elimination and must win four consecutive games to complete an improbable comeback.
The Rays will turn to SP Griffin Jax in Game 4, hoping the right-hander can slow down a Brewers lineup that has dominated the World Series. Milwaukee has not announced its starting pitcher, potentially setting up another bullpen game as the club looks to complete the sweep.
Below, we'll break down our Brewers vs. Rays prediction and picks for Tuesday's World Series Game 4, including the winner and player picks for PrizePicks.
{{mlb_offer_banner="/style-system/ui-components-playbook"}}
Brewers vs. Rays Prediction, Winner Payout, Over/Under for World Series Game 4
Milwaukee enters Game 4 as the road favorite, returning a 1.75x payout if it wins outright.
Here are the full payouts for the Brewers vs. Rays game. PrizePicks data is live at the time of writing and is subject to change.
Make your Brewers vs. Rays prediction on the winner on PrizePicks.
Unless otherwise noted, data used in this article is from FanGraphs, Baseball Savant, and MLB.com.
Griffin Jax (3.41 xFIP) will take the ball for Tampa Bay as the Rays' season hangs in the balance. The right-hander finished the regular season 8-10 with a 3.53 ERA and 116 strikeouts.
He faces a tough assignment against a Milwaukee offense that has consistently put runners on base throughout the World Series, but his regular-season home success could help him tonight.
Jax has struggled during the postseason, allowing 4 earned runs over six innings in his previous playoff appearances.
We can talk all we want about Tampa’s pitching plans, but ultimately the Rays offense will need a much better showing against Milwaukee's pitching staff if they want to save their season.
Despite being so good at getting runners on base and capitalizing with runners in scoring position during the regular season, the Rays managed just 1 run and struggled to generate sustained offense in Game 3. Those same issues plagued Tampa Bay in the first two games of this series.
The Brewers' pitching plans remain uncertain heading into tonight. Milwaukee has not announced a starter, and a bullpen-heavy approach seems most likely with the championship within reach.
The Brewers used LHP Robert Gasser in Game 3, and he delivered one of the postseason's most dominant starts, allowing just 1 hit over six innings while striking out 6.
Gasser's performance gave Milwaukee's bullpen valuable rest, which could prove significant if the Brewers need multiple relievers to get through Game 4. Milwaukee's pitching staff has been outstanding throughout the postseason, allowing just 7 runs across its first three World Series games.
The Brewers offense has stolen the show this World Series. At one point last night, they recorded eight straight two-out hits to blow the game wide open — a truly magnificent team feat on the grandest stage of all.
{{mlb_offer_banner="/style-system/ui-components-playbook"}}
Brewers vs. Rays Prediction on Winner for World Series Game 4 – 10/27/26
Here are the key stats and trends behind our Brewers vs. Rays prediction on the winner for Tuesday's World Series Game 4.
- It feels insane to fade this Brewers team right now, but I can’t see Tampa Bay getting swept at home, especially considering how dominant its been at Tropicana Field all season.
- The Rays went 58-27-0 at home this season; their 68.2% home win rate ranked second in baseball, behind the Brewers.
- Griffin Jax's regular-season home xFIP was 2.82, a full run better than his 4.08 road xFIP.
- The Brewers didn’t need to use any of their high-leverage arms last night, and neither did the Rays, who essentially conceded the game in the fifth inning. This leaves Tampa Bay’s best relievers ready to come in, and perhaps used slightly more aggressively than Milwaukee’s, given the lack of margin for error in an elimination game.
- While the Brewers’ pen has been awesome this postseason, their 3.57 xFIP sits well above a 1.34 ERA. Also, their .220 BABIP could signal regression in what is shaping up to be a bullpen game for the Brew Crew.
- The Rays offense has been better at home, owning a 108 wRC+ at the Trop compared to a 100 wRC+ on the road during the regular season.
Brewers vs. Rays Picks, Player Stats for World Series on PrizePicks – 10/27/26
Here are two Brewers vs. Rays player picks to consider on PrizePicks for Tuesday's World Series Game 4. Today's MLB picks include Jackson Chourio and Griffin Jax.
Brewers OF Jackson Chourio vs. Rays: 7.5 Hitter Fantasy Score
- This guy is simply unfadeable right now. He's recorded three straight multi-hit games to start the World Series and cleared this projection in all three as well.
- He has also cleared this projection in eight of the Brewers' 11 postseason games (72.7%).
- After recording no steals in any game before the World Series, Chourio has shown more willingness to run, already swiping 3 bags in this series, giving him yet another way to clear this projection.
- Jax was a reverse-splits pitcher this season, with a 10.26 K/9 and 3.08 xFIP vs. LHH compared to only a 7.88 K/9 and 3.89 xFIP vs. RHH.
- It may not matter who pitches for the Rays against Chourio, as Jackson owns a .333 batting average across 39 lifetime at-bats against this Rays pitching staff.
Rays P Griffin Jax vs. Brewers: 3.5 Strikeouts
- Jax owns some of the most insane home/road splits in baseball. He owned an 11.55 K/9 at home during the regular season, compared to a 6.71 K/9 on the road.
- He has specifically dominated LHB, striking them out to the tune of a 12.92 K/9 to go along with a 2.12 xFIP at home this season. The Brewers lineup projects to have six left-handed hitters tonight.
- Of those six left-handed hitters, four had a regular-season strikeout rate above 25.1%.
- While his leash may not be long, he can give it his all while he is in there, and after 12 days off, he should be rested and ready to give max effort.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Blue Jays' Alejandro Kirk's Decision Draws Personal Message From Best Friend's Dad
item.dc:creator: Dibyendu Mondal

item.content:encoded:
Toronto Blue Jays catcher Alejandro Kirk attended Game 3 of the World Series on Monday night at Tropicana Field.
Kirk and his wife, Sofia Castañeda, went to cheer on his childhood best friend, Tampa Bay Rays first baseman Jonathan Aranda. Castañeda shared the moment on Instagram.
It was the second straight round in which Kirk watched Aranda in person. Aranda’s father also spoke about the two friends and their long road together.
Jonathan Aranda’s Dad Sends Touching Message About Alejandro Kirk
Humberto Aranda, Jonathan’s father, attended Game 3 as well. He spoke with Mexican media about his son and Kirk during the World Series.
“Definitely seeing Alejandro, seeing Jonathan, seeing them here after so many years of following them… they played together, they started playing together at the age of three and this path that they are still following together is completely rewarding,” he said. “And for the families, for both families, the journey has been very good, very beautiful, and we are very happy to be able to live the experience.”
Humberto was an assistant coach on the boys’ Little League team in Tijuana, Mexico. Kirk’s father, Juan Manuel Kirk, managed that team.
Kirk and Aranda have been friends since they were 3. They played on the same youth teams for 12 years. They still work out at the same gym in Tijuana.
The friends traded places this fall. Last October, Aranda watched from the stands as Kirk played in the World Series. He wore a jersey from their old Tijuana youth team, the Glu-Glu, with a World Series patch.
When Kirk homered in Game 1, Aranda started a social media campaign to recover the ball. “It was a big thing for me to go see him,” Aranda said during the ALCS.
Now Kirk is returning the favor.
Alejandro Kirk Also Watched Aranda Clinch the Pennant at Tropicana Field
Monday was not Kirk’s first trip to Tropicana Field this postseason. He attended Game 6 of the American League Championship Series on Oct. 19.
Kirk has been keeping up with games at Tropicana Field. He has been in the area for work. He has been training at the Blue Jays’ player development complex in Dunedin, Florida.
Kirk was spotted at the complex on Oct. 23, getting an early start on the 2027 season. The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1. A lockout after that date would bar players on 40-man rosters from team facilities.

item.title: [Blog Red Machine] Reds get laughable Randy Arozarena suggestion from someone who should know better
item.dc:creator: Drew Koch
item.description: Jim Bowden was the general manager of the Cincinnati Reds for almost 11 years. item.content:encoded:
Jim Bowden was the general manager of the Cincinnati Reds for almost 11 years. Nowadays, he moonlights as some sort of MLB insider, appearing on various podcasts while also writing for The Athletic. Bowden's latest column featured the top-40 MLB free agents with contract predictions and team fits. Hilariously, Bowden named the Reds as a "fit" for Randy Arozarena.
Okay, Jim, we'll play along. Yes, the Reds would undoubtedly love to have Arozarena's bat in the middle of their lineup next season. Few free agent hitters offer the type of upside that Arozarena could bring. He hit .281/.381/.484 with 26 home runs, 79 RBI, 26 stolen bases, and a 148 OPS+ with the Seattle Mariners last season.
Arozarena is a three-time All-Star who's right-handed bat would be a perfect fit in the Reds' left-handed heavy outfield. His defense doesn't necessarily fit Terry Francona's emphasis on playing "clean baseball", but Tito would probably make an exception if it meant having another dynamic bat to match the hitting prowess of Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart in 2027.
You know, Jim, you might be onto something here. Arozarena would be a terrific fit for the Reds this offseason. How much would it take to sign him? Oh!
Randy Arozarena to the Reds falls apart the moment you see the price tag
You see, that's where Bowden's idea falls off a cliff. The contract prediction for Arozarena is five years at $124 million. That's a $24.8 million AAV, just south of what Joey Votto was making during his last few years in a Reds uniform.
The fact that Bowden even mentioned the Reds as a possible fit just reveals how invalid his opinion is. While he didn't work under the Castellini during his time with the Reds, he knows better than anybody that Cincinnati doesn't have the resources to pursue a player like Arozarena in free agency.
Yes, the Reds targeted Kyle Schwarber last winter, but as every fan throughout the tri-state knows, that was a one-off situation. Cincinnati was trying to lure the Middletown native back home and reportedly offered him a five-year, $125 million. Schwarber eventually re-signed with the Philadelphia Phillies, and the Reds never pivoted to another big bat like Pete Alonso, Alex Bregman, or Cody Bellinger.
Listing Arozarena as a "best fit" for the Reds is like suggesting a Rolls-Royce is the best fit for a line cook at a fast food restaurant. It's just not going to happen. Try again, Jimbo.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Boston Red Sox Free Agency: Could Red Sox Enter Bidding War for Top Japanese Slugger?
item.dc:creator: Zach Coe

item.content:encoded:
One insider projects a big-market bidding war for free-agent slugger Teruaki Sato.
With the Milwaukee Brewers holding a commanding 3-0 series lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series, the offseason is officially on the doorstep. As the Boston Red Sox put the finishing touches on their offseason plan, one insider, former Cincinnati Reds and Washington Nationals GM and The Athletic writer Jim Bowden, projects a “big market bidding war,” including Boston, for top international free agent, third baseman Teruaki Sato.
About Sato
The 27-year-old spent most of 2026 at third base with the Hanshin Tigers in NPB. In 143 games, Sato hit .306/.383/.609/.991, led the league with 40 doubles, 39 home runs, and 106 runs driven in. Sato has some concerns, though: he struck out at a 26.7 percent rate in 2026, the third-highest in NPB. However, an 11.1 percent walk rate offset that somewhat; it was the ninth-highest in the league.
Defensively, Sato profiles as a below-average third baseman. He also spent time in right field in 2026, where he was also below average. Ultimately, the 27-year-old could find a long-term home at first base or as a designated hitter.
Hanshin posted Sato on Oct. 19; he has 45 days to sign with a team. However, that clock will pause at the start of the lockout on Dec. 1 at 11:59 p.m. ET if he is not signed by then.
What did Bowden say?
“Some teams believe he can stay at third base; others see him as best suited for first base or left field. Either way, the bat profiles for the middle of the order. I think he stays at third base initially and would be a perfect fit for teams like the Phillies, Red Sox, Angels and Yankees, which leads me to believe this will end up being a big-market bidding war,” Bowden wrote on Tuesday.
Will the Red Sox spend that much on Sato?
Put me in the camp that is skeptical that Sato will land a deal that pays him $36 million annually, even if a bidding war emerges among the big-market teams Bowden lists as potential suitors. It is worth noting that both Chicago White Sox first baseman Munetaka Murakami and Toronto Blue Jays third baseman Kazuma Okamoto were projected to land much higher deals than the ones they eventually signed (two-year, $34-million for Murakami and four-year, $60 for Okamoto).
Murakami faced concerns similar to Sato's about his strikeout rate and how it would translate to Major League Baseball. While Murakami struck out 35.4 percent of the time, the second-highest rate in baseball, he also hit 35 home runs, posted a .478 slugging percentage, and walked 16.6 percent of plate appearances. Murakami’s success in Chicago will surely help Sato’s market, but not by $19 million more annually.
While Bowden projects Sato will stay at third base, Boston already has the likely Gold Glove Award winner at the position in Caleb Durbin. They’ll want to stick with him at the hot corner after building so much of their team identity on pitching and defense. With All-Star Willson Contreras handling first base, Sato would likely be a designated hitter in Boston at least for the remainder of Contreras’ contract, which has a team option for 2028.
Now, financially, the Red Sox are in a precarious spot. With $268 million committed to 2027 before any additions, the team projects to be over the second-luxury tax threshold for what would be the third straight season. With so much of the financial landscape in flux due to the ongoing labor negotiations, it seems unlikely the team will add significant money before the lockout without first moving some money off the books. That said, if Sato’s market is closer to the $25-million AAV Spotrac projects, the 27-year-old seems like an ideal target for Boston.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Guardians Face Major Steven Kwan Decision as Trade Rumors Loom
item.dc:creator: Steve Kubitza; Unknown
item.description: The Cleveland Guardians once again have a series of roster decisions to make. That remains true whether there is a lockout or not. item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Guardians once again have a series of roster decisions to make. That remains true whether there is a lockout or not.
One player in particular who will be in focus all offseason is Steven Kwan. He and the team have not come to terms on any long-term extension and he is entering his final year of arbitration in 2027. After that, he's a free agent.
This leaves the team with several options in terms of what to do with the perennial Gold Glove winner.
Guardians have two logical options with Steven Kwan
One route the team could take is to trade Kwan this offseason. MLB Trade Rumors pegged his arbitration value at $11.3 million for 2027. That is a bargain for a team willing to spend more than the Guardians do on an annual basis.
An offseason trade would also bring back much more value than a midseason deal, making this the first logical option. However, the impending lockout presents a potential caveat to all the trade talk.
There is the possibility MLB institutes both a salary cap and a salary floor. The latter would ensure teams spend a certain amount each season. Such a floor being put in place would immediately mean the Guardians would have to sign some players to meet the threshold, given the team's frugal ways in 2026. That is where a Kwan extension could come into play just to hit that mark.
The cap and floor are, however, contentious issues among players and owners, so that scenario is not a given.
The simplest plan of all would be to sign Kwan to an extension before the 2027 season begins. His final year of arbitration could be bought out and the player could be rewarded for his years of success.
It all just truly depends on the whims of ownership and how much they are willing to spend. Kwan got off to a horrible start in 2026, but rebounded to finish with a 5.3-bWAR season.
Chase DeLauter, Angel Martinez, and even Petey Halpin are all options in the outfield. DeLauter, of course, is the main piece of that trio. Jo Adell could be another piece as well if the Guardians decide to keep him in town in his final year of arbitration.
Top prospect Ralphy Velazquez can play left field as well, though him ending up at first base seems to be the ideal plan.
Trading Kwan away could bring back a set of elite prospects in return. Yet the Guardians already have a logjam at several positions and Kwan is a proven, reliable talent who is still only 29 years old.
This will be a unique MLB offseason and one that could lead to monumental changes for how the Guardians pay players. That puts the impending Kwan decision potentially in limbo until we all see the final outcome between the players and the owners.
Steve is a lifelong Cleveland sports fan who proudly wears his Guardians, Browns, and Cavs gear in his current home of Santa Barbara. He has covered Cleveland sports online for the past decade and is still waiting for the Browns to draft a QB who signs a second contract in town.
Follow kubitzawrites

item.title: [North Side Baseball] How Alex Bregman's Arrival Brought Dansby Swanson Back to the Shortstop Upper Crust—For Now
item.dc:creator: Matthew Trueblood

item.content:encoded:
Cubs Video
What Alex Bregman can do on the field—the statistical contribution he can make when it's his turn to bat and when the ball is hit his way—is plenty valuable. By the end of the 2026 season, that was obvious. Bregman was one of the best hitters in baseball from mid-July onward, and he won the Fielding Bible Award at third base for his supernal defense. Multiple teams were willing to give him a fat five-year deal last offseason, and most of that money is for the way he hits and fields.
However, Bregman also has enormous value as a facilitator, a leader, and an organization changer. That's what made the Cubs willing to outbid the Red Sox and others for his services; it was the extra cushion they needed to feel safe spashing so much money on a player who would turn 32 just days after playing his first regular-season game for them. In those areas, he was arguably an even greater success in 2026 than on the stat sheet. The partnership of Bregman and Pete Crow-Armstrong, offensively, was about more than the fact that they hit back-to-back at the top of the lineup 24 times. They made improvements that followed the same patterns. They communicated about what they were seeing from each opposing pitcher. Bregman thrived down the stretch, but his input also helped Crow-Armstrong break the game, even while the veteran was still mired in a long early funk.
Defensively, his partnership would be with shortstop Dansby Swanson. Bregman replaced Swanson as the highest-paid player on the team and as the team's resident emblem of intention to win and dedication to whatever that takes. Swanson was the first overall pick in 2015; Bregman was the second. Swanson won the 2021 World Series with the team from near Atlanta. Bregman won the World Baseball Classic and the Series in 2017, then another Series in 2022. Swanson's championship came at Bregman's expense, too, as his club beat Houston in that Fall Classic. The two players' history was interwoven, and they would need to prove they could achieve as much together as they had (seemingly) working at odds, to top one another.
It couldn't have worked out more beautifully, or in a fashion more quintessentially Bregman. Here's the gist: In 2025, Swanson's defensive numbers dipped. That wasn't surprising. He was 31 years old, which is already getting a bit old for a shortstop in the majors today. He doesn't have an elite arm (or even, in truth, an average one), and though he learned long ago to get rid of the ball exceptionally quickly when needed, that can't make up for everything. He suffered, in particular, on exactly the balls you would expect an aging non-premium athlete to suffer on: ones hit to his right, where he had to range into the hole and make the toughest plays asked of shortstops. According to Baseball Savant, Swanson dropped from 16 and 12 runs saved in 2023 and 2024, respectively, to just 2 in 2025. The biggest difference came on balls that forced him to move toward third base:
- 2023: 8 Outs Above Average
- 2024: 2
- 2025: -1
The Cubs didn't do what many teams might have done in such a situation, though. First of all, they didn't even briefly consider moving Swanson to second base and trading Nico Hoerner. That would have been a viable option; Hoerner was an impending free agent until he signed a six-year extension last spring. The Cubs believed Swanson could still be a great defensive shortstop, though, and that Hoerner's defensive work as his double-play partner was too valuable to lose.
Even with the same personnel in place, though, they could have more aggressively shaded their infield alignments, putting Swanson a step or two closer to the hole when there was a chance he would be called upon to make a play there. Instead, they used fairly traditional setups. The 2025 Cubs were 17th in shading their infield, doing so 53% of the time against left-handed batters and 6% of the time against righties. That led to a lot of plays that looked like this.
Seeing the ball zip past Swanson like that makes him seem slow, but that's unfair. Alec Bohm hit that grounder at 104 miles per hour. To make the play, Swanson needed to be a step farther in the direction he had to go. Failing that, not even a younger, more explosive player would get there. But the even more telling plays, perhaps, were those that looked more like this.
This ball isn't hit so hard, and Swanson has the quick feet to run it down. However, because he started at a neutral position, he had to run an extra step or two before snaring the bounce. That meant throwing off-balance, on the run, which robbed him of the ability to be accurate and powerful. This is where being 31 and a bit less strong-armed than most shortstops caught up to him, but much of the reason was his starting position.
Early in 2026, the same thing was happening too often. Swanson would flag down a ball that seemed ticketed for left field, but because he did so at the very edge of his range, he still couldn't record an out.
Over time, though, a (literal) shift took place. Bregman, who played with one of the game's most aggressive shifting teams in Houston before the league outlawed the true shift, advocated for a bit more proactive shading with his new club. They didn't become an extreme team, but they did become one of the league leaders in that area. In 2026, the Cubs shaded their infield 67% of the time against lefties and 14% of the time against righties, moving them into the top seven in shading, overall. Swanson started making plays that he couldn't make the previous year.
There were balls, like the one above, that would have been clean singles to left field in 2025 but became great plays in 2026. There were also plenty that might have become infield hits in 2025, but which ended up looking routine this year.
Swanson's numbers rebounded, especially on those balls that took him toward third base: he got back to 8 OAA on them. The way OAA tabulates value, that actually took a bite out of Bregman. He rated worse (-6 OAA) on balls to his left than he ever has before. But Bregman didn't care. By playing closer to the line against right-handed batters, he was better able to set himself for long throws when he made a play along the foul line, and he got better coming in on slowly hit balls. He was the best he's ever been at third, precisely because he ceded a bit of range to his superb partner on the left side of the infield.
Communication between those two players is more important than many who watch the game from home might realize. They don't call each other off in quite the same way outfielders do, but there has to be an understanding between the shortstop and the third baseman: when to take a ball and when to let it go; whether your partner will break to cover a base, and how to back them up if they go for the ball instead; where your teammate should throw the ball, if fielding it took him in a direction that makes it hard for him to see the whole diamond. Bregman and Swanson worked gloriously together in their first year as a tandem, which helped the Cubs reach the postseason and provided hope for the short-term aging profile of each.
That doesn't mean it won't get harder. As each moves into his mid-30s, they'll have to continue communicating, adapting and adjusting. Working together is important, but it can't entirely make up for the fact that each individual is getting a bit older, a bit slower and a bit less able to react in the blink of an eye. Next year, the Cubs' infield defense will probably be worse. That's the nature of investing so much in players who would ordinarily move off their positions, and slotting them into a roster that doesn't permit them to do so. What we saw in the first year of Bregman and Swanson, though, is that they're likely to weather those degradations better than most, because of their savvy and their shared commitment to doing whatever it takes to win.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] World Series 2026: Brewers' DH Christian Yelich turns pivotal play of World Series Game 3 with speed and instincts — 'Nobody cares about baserunning more than him'
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG — The Brewers won by a mile because they're obsessed with the inches.
Nobody would describe the final outcome of Milwaukee's emphatic beatdown on Monday — a 10-1 drubbing of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the World Series — as "close." Not since 2015 has there been a larger margin of victory in a World Series game. The Brewers' 16-to-3 hit advantage over the flailing Rays was the third-largest in Fall Classic history. Starter Robert Gasser allowed just one one hit and faced the minimum across six brilliant innings, becoming the first lefty to do that in a World Series game since Sandy Koufax in 1965. A massive gathering of Brewers fans, an estimated 30% of the crowd, was there to witness it all, their voices joyously hoarse by the end.
It was a shellacking of historic proportions.
But Milwaukee's commanding 3-0 series lead, one that places this franchise on the precipice of its first championship, was earned in the margins on a bang-bang play that folks in the Badger State will remember for a long time.
Up a pair in the top of the fifth, the Brewers put runners on first and second against Tampa Bay starter Freddy Peralta. Milwaukee catcher William Contreras, the best hitter in these playoffs, ripped a two-hopper toward third baseman Junior Caminero. In a spinning motion, Tampa's talented talisman snagged the pearl and flicked it to second baseman Ben Williamson as a full-bore Christian Yelich slid into the bag. Umpire Dan Bellino punched his fist. The FOX graphic evaporated from the screen. Multiple members of Tampa Bay's between-innings hype squad jogged onto the outfield track for some type of giveaway.
Yelich, though, clung to the bag with his left hand as he motioned adamantly toward Belino with his right.
"Safe, safe."
Safe, indeed.
The Brewers challenged the call. Before Bellino could finish announcing the overturn, Tampa Bay skipper Kevin Cash was already headed toward the mound to pull Peralta.
But no move, at that point, could have stopped the inevitable.
"The whole game was changed when Yeli was safe at second," Brewer manager Pat Murphy insisted afterwards. "That's just a hustle play. When your leader makes that play, that says it all. The game was changed because he did a little thing that anybody can do."
Yelich, by beating the throw to second, turned a dead frame into the inning of a lifetime. The floodgates soon burst, sweeping away Tampa's next pitcher, Cam Booser. On a 2-2 count, he served a mid-zone fastball to second baseman Brice Turang, who scorched one off shortstop Taylor Walls' glove and into the outfield. Milwaukee's lead was doubled.
As the sizable traveling contingent — a bar down the street sold out of Miller Lite before first pitch — went berzerk, the Fox broadcast panned to a young Rays fan, who could be seen uttering to his companion a harsh and humbling realization: "That's the series."
Milwaukee, though, would leave no doubt. And then some.
Their next five batters all found grass, with each consequential hit eliciting louder and louder roars from the armada of traveling Wisconsinites. In total, the Brewers strung together seven consecutive two-out hits to plate eight two-out runs, a World Series record. It was an all-time heater and a fitting performance from a pridefully selfless Brewers offense that has prioritized passing the baton over hitting big flies all season long.
"Nobody wants to be the hero," hitting coach Dan Vogelbach boasted.
That might be true, but Yelich, with his mad dash to second, was the under-the-radar hero of this evening.
With the right-handed Contreras at the plate and a runner on second, Rays first baseman Ryan Villade was shaded toward second, opting not to hold Yelich on. That allowed the Brewers' captain to take a much larger-than-average lead off first base. By the time Contreras swung, Yelich was already about 30 feet from the bag, his right foot in the air ready to break in either direction. As the ball bounced toward Caminero, Yelich landed and broke hard for second.
"You have to understand where you're at in space," Yelich explained postgame. "You're lengthening your primary [lead] in case there's a ball in the hole or some sort of play happens where you could potentially beat the throw."
It was a sublime bit of baserunning, the kind that takes years of purposeful, monotonous practice to get good at. There's also an element of internal pre-pitch preparation: "If X happens, I do Y." Yelich executed that process perfectly. Caminero, who had ample time to get the slow-footed Contreras at first, did not.
"The beauty of it is that you have guys like Yeli that demand it from the group," first-base coach Spencer Allen told Yahoo Sports about the team's attention to detail.
Jason Lane, Milwaukee's offense and strategy coordinator, explained to Yahoo Sports that he tells players to approach a secondary lead at first base and two outs with the same intent and intensity they would bring to a "contact play." That's the inside-baseball term for when a runner at third, with the infield drawn in, plans to race home on contact — no matter where the ball's hit.
"When you remind guys of that and explain it to them like that — and these guys are hunting all those little things that we preach about right turns — it can become something that happens in a playoff game," he explained.
On a team that cares deeply about the little things, Yelich, the group's most accomplished character, might care most of all. That establishes a standard, one that has helped push the Brewers to an amazing 10-1 record this postseason. But that crucial play, and its outcome, was about more than Yelich's impressive read and instincts. His footspeed from first to second clocked in at 28.5 mph, a full tick faster than his season average. That's an 81st-percentile result from a 34-year-old DH with a history of back problems.
Yelich was once a speedster before age and injuries did their thing. There exists a timeline in which the 2018 MVP evolved into a bat-first baseclogger, a plodder focused on in-box responsibilities. Instead, Yelich has done everything in his power to remain as athletic, as lithe and as quick as possible. Years of treatment, offseason sprint work, healthy habits, weight room sessions — all of it has allowed Yelich to maintain his speed despite the barrage of injuries and his status as a primary DH.
"I've got some things that have happened to me, but for the most part, I feel pretty good," he said when asked about his speed. "I feel like I can still hang with the boys out there."
The boys agree.
"That baserunning by Yeli there, which allowed us to have that huge inning ..." outfielder Sal Frelick said. "We work on those things in spring. He's the guy that's running the meeting, saying this is important. It's his 14th season. He's been All-Star, Silver Slugger, MVP, and nobody cares about baserunning more than him. Just to see him do that, get a good secondary, run as hard as he could and beat that out — that's what allowed us to have that big inning."
"Little things like that — that's what makes our team great."
Great might be an understatement. If the Brewers finish the deal in Game 4, they would become the first team in the League Championship Series era to sweep both the championship series and World Series rounds. They would finish this month a mind-boggling 11-1, with their only defeat coming by one run in NLDS Game 3 in San Diego. There's a strong argument that we are currently witnessing the most dominant postseason team in MLB history.
The gap between these Brewers and the rest of the league is a massive chasm, yes, but it's one they chiseled one swing and one step at a time.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are favored to take Game 3 on Monday, but their chances of capturing their first ever World Series title have dwindled.
The Rays jumped out to a 4-0 first inning lead in Game 2, but through the game’s final eight innings the offense sputtered and the defense, nor pitching from ace Drew Rasmussen, was as sharp as needed to hold down the Brewers, who earned a 5-4 victory.
The pair of one-run victories in Milwaukee have put the Brewers in prime position for their first title. Nearly 81% of MLB teams that have generated a 2-0 series lead in the World Series have gone on to win the title.
To disrupt that statistic, the Rays will need to find a way to win Game 3. Kalshi traders make their odds 53% as of Monday morning.
For informational purposes only. Not trading advice. See full disclaimer below. Kalshi is the Official Prediction Market Partner of the Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Dodgers, San Francisco Giants, San Diego Padres, and Boston Red Sox.
World Series Game 3 Odds: Rays favored in home ballpark
Right-handed pitcher Freddy Peralta had a rough start to his 2026 campaign when pitching for the New York Mets. But after being dealt to the Rays, he’s unlocked a former version of himself, one the Milwaukee Brewers know quite well. Peralta pitched for the Brewers for eight seasons before being traded to the Mets in the offseason. The Mets dealt him to the Rays at the trade deadline.
As such, now he’ll need to square off against his former team in World Series Game 3, looking to extend an incredible stretch of pitching which saw him earn ALCS MVP honors.
Across three starts and one relief appearance this postseason, Peralta has thrown 16.2 innings and allowed just two earned runs, good for a 1.08 ERA.
But the Brewers represent a level up offensively. Milwaukee finished the regular season tied for first in wRC+ against right-handed starters and led the league in on-base percentage and batting average against the handedness.
On the other hand, the Rays will draw left-handed starter Robert Gasser. Like the rest of the Milwaukee staff, Gasser has been fantastic this postseason, throwing nine innings over the course of two starts and allowing just one earned run.
Southpaws have been a challenge for the Rays this season, with the team ranking 26th against lefties in terms of wRC+ during the regular season. Even if they are able to get through Gasser, the Milwaukee bullpen features lefties JoJo Romero, DL Hall, and Aaron Ashby, and has been nearly unhittable, collectively posting a 1.23 ERA in nearly 51 innings this postseason.
Nevertheless, Kalshi traders make the Rays, who posted a 55-26 record at home during the regular season, slight favorites at 53% in Game 3.
The Rays overcame a 2-1 deficit in the ALCS, but they face a stiffer test against baseball’s top team in the World Series.
Regardless of the Game 3 winner, Game 4 will take place on Tuesday in Tampa Bay. In early trading, Kalshi traders make the Brewers slight favorites on the road in that game, pricing them at 50%.
Should a Game 5 be necessary, it will take place on Wednesday in Tampa Bay. If Games 6 or 7 are required, those will take place back in Milwaukee after a travel day.
Through two games, Brewers catcher William Contreras is the favorite for World Series MVP, according to Kalshi traders.
Contreras is trading around 38% to earn the award while outfielder Jackson Chourio is trading at 17% and left-handed reliever Aaron Ashby is priced at 15%.
In their two home victories, Contreras has notched four hits in eight at-bats and driven in two runs for Milwaukee. Plus, he’s thrown out multiple runners attempting to steal and helped manage a pitching staff through two tense one-run victories.
Chourio has posted similar stats, netting four hits in his nine at-bats, while stealing two bases and cutting down a runner at the plate with an outfield assist during Game 2.
Though less heralded coming into the series, Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby has been dominant all postseason, pitching 15.2 innings without allowing a single run. That includes more than three innings of World Series play in which he’s only allowed one hit.
Down 2-0, the highest priced Ray player is Junior Caminero, who is trading around 6% to win the award.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Francisco Lindor Wins 2026 Roberto Clemente Award, Continuing a Proud Puerto Rican Legacy
item.dc:creator: Eddie Lennon; Staff Writer
item.description: Francisco Lindor has accomplished just about everything a baseball player could hope to achieve. He's a five-time All-Star, a four-time Silver Slugger and one of the most recognizable shortstops in Major League Baseball. But on October 26, Lindor received an honor that has little to do with his numbers at the plate or his performance on the field. The New York Mets star was named the 2026 recipient of the Roberto Clemente Award, Major League Baseball's highest individual honor for a player's cha
item.content:encoded:
Francisco Lindor has accomplished just about everything a baseball player could hope to achieve. He's a five-time All-Star, a four-time Silver Slugger and one of the most recognizable shortstops in Major League Baseball.
But on October 26, Lindor received an honor that has little to do with his numbers at the plate or his performance on the field.
The New York Mets star was named the 2026 recipient of the Roberto Clemente Award, Major League Baseball's highest individual honor for a player's character, philanthropy and community impact.
For Lindor, the recognition carries an additional layer of meaning. He's a proud Puerto Rican native who grew up learning about Clemente, the legendary Hall of Famer whose impact on baseball extended far beyond the diamond.
Now, Lindor joins the group of players whose actions have helped carry that legacy forward.
Francisco Lindor's Roberto Clemente Award Is About More Than Baseball
The Roberto Clemente Award recognizes the MLB player who best represents baseball through community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions on and off the field.
Clemente, a 15-time All-Star and one of baseball's greatest players, died on December 31, 1972, while traveling to deliver humanitarian aid to earthquake victims in Nicaragua.
His commitment to helping others became inseparable from his legacy.
For Lindor, that example began long before he reached the Major Leagues.
Growing up in Puerto Rico, he learned about Clemente's career and humanitarian efforts in school. Lindor has spoken about how Clemente inspired him to use his own platform to help others.
Lindor is the fifth Puerto Rican-born player to win the award, joining Edgar Martínez, Carlos Delgado, Carlos Beltrán and Yadier Molina.
That connection makes this recognition particularly significant. Puerto Rico has a rich baseball tradition, and Clemente remains one of its most influential figures. Lindor's award recognizes not only his individual work but also the continuing influence of a Puerto Rican icon whose example transcends generations.
Lindor's Charity Work Starts With Education
One of the clearest examples of Lindor's philanthropy is his commitment to education.
Since 2020, he has donated more than $1 million to Montverde Academy in Florida, his alma mater, helping fund Lindor Hall, a two-story middle school building featuring science and technology laboratories.
He also established the Francisco Lindor Scholarship Fund to help students who otherwise might not have the financial means to attend the school.
His involvement goes beyond writing checks. Lindor remains engaged with students through mentorship, career guidance and youth baseball initiatives.
That commitment reflects an important part of his charitable work: creating opportunities that can continue to benefit young people long after a particular event or donation.
Giving Back to Puerto Rico
Lindor's connection to his home island has also shaped his response to natural disasters.
Following Hurricanes Maria in 2017 and Fiona in 2022, he provided financial support for relief efforts in Puerto Rico. He has also helped restore athletic facilities in his hometown of Caguas and hosted youth baseball clinics.
These efforts connect his philanthropic work to the communities that helped shape him.
For Puerto Rican athletes who reach the highest levels of professional sports, success can provide an opportunity to give back to the places where their journeys began. Lindor has used that opportunity to support recovery efforts, youth development and access to sports.
His work also includes partnerships focused on environmental conservation and ongoing community support.
Making a Difference in Queens
Lindor's impact isn't limited to Puerto Rico or his former school.
In New York, he and his wife, Katia, have supported programs designed to help children and families. Their initiatives include annual back-to-school efforts with New Balance that provide hundreds of students with backpacks and essential school supplies.
Lindor also launched Lindor's Leaders in 2026, a year-long leadership development program for students in Bayside High School's Sports Medicine Program.
The initiative focuses on mental health, communication, teamwork and leadership. Lindor personally mentors participating students, helping them develop skills they can apply in school and throughout their lives.
He has also worked with Children's Miracle Network Hospitals, Special Olympics Florida and organizations supporting youth and families navigating disability.
On the field, Lindor represents the Mets. In the community, his work reaches far beyond the team's fan base.
A $100,000 Boost for the SEEN Foundation
The 2026 award also brings additional support for a cause Lindor and his wife have embraced.
Capital One is donating $100,000 to the SEEN Foundation in honor of Lindor's achievement. The organization works to empower young people, create opportunities and strengthen communities, including supporting families with children navigating physical disabilities.
The contribution gives Lindor's recognition a direct charitable impact, helping support an organization whose mission aligns with the couple's philanthropic efforts.
It's a fitting addition to an award designed not simply to celebrate what a player has done, but to help extend the impact of that work.
Carrying Roberto Clemente's Legacy Forward
There is no shortage of ways to measure Lindor's baseball career. His offensive production, defense, leadership and importance to the Mets will continue to shape how his playing days are remembered.
The Roberto Clemente Award recognizes a different side of that career.
Lindor has invested in education, supported Puerto Rico after devastating hurricanes, mentored students and helped provide opportunities for children and families in New York. These are tangible efforts that extend his influence beyond the ballpark.
His Puerto Rican heritage makes the honor particularly meaningful because Clemente's legacy has long been part of the island's baseball identity. Lindor grew up learning about Clemente's commitment to service, and he now has an opportunity to inspire the next generation in a similar way.
Winning the Roberto Clemente Award is not just another milestone for Francisco Lindor. It's recognition of the person he has chosen to be away from baseball.
For the Mets, Puerto Rico and the broader baseball community, that may be one of his most meaningful accomplishments yet.

item.description: New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor has won the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award, Major League Baseball announced. This award is given annually to the player "who best represents the game of Baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field. item.content:encoded:
New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor has won the 2026 Roberto Clemente Award, Major League Baseball announced.
This award is given annually to the player "who best represents the game of Baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.
Each team nominates one player, similar to the NFL's Walter Payton Man of the Year Award.
Lindor earned the award for his contributions to education, youth leadership and disaster relief in Puerto Rico, according to a league statement. As part of Lindor's winning the award, Capital One will be donating $100,000 to the SEEN Foundation in Lindor's honor. The SEEN Foundation "empowers youth, create opportunities and foster positive community impact" among families dealing with disabilities.
Here are the other charitable efforts the league highlighted in its statement.
- "Lindor's Leaders Program (est. 2026) — Launched in partnership with New Balance, this year-long leadership development initiative for students in Bayside High School's Sports Medicine Program focuses on mental health, communication, teamwork, and leadership. Lindor personally mentors participating students, equipping them with the confidence to lead in their schools and communities.
- Support for Children's Miracle Network Hospitals — In 2026, Francisco partnered with Dairy Queen and Children's Miracle Network Hospitals for Miracle Treat Day, raising critical funds for local children's hospitals by donating directly to families in need $1 or more from every Blizzard Treat sold.
- Transformative Commitment to Education — A proud graduate of Montverde Academy, Lindor has donated more than $1 million since 2020 to build Lindor Hall, a two-story middle school building featuring state-of-the-art science and technology labs. He also established the Francisco Lindor Scholarship Fund to provide financial aid for students, remaining personally involved through mentorship, career guidance, annual PLAY BALL youth events, and equipment donations for the school's baseball team.
- Disaster Relief and Advocacy for Puerto Rico — Deeply committed to his native Puerto Rico, Francisco provided essential financial support following Hurricanes Maria and Fiona, restored athletic facilities in his hometown of Caguas, and hosted youth clinics. He continues to partner with organizations including Team Rubicon, the Amazin' Mets Foundation, Players for the Planet, and Rescate Playas Borinquen for ongoing recovery and environmental conservation.
- Serving the Queens Community — Through an annual back-to-school initiative with New Balance, Lindor provides hundreds of students each year with backpacks and essential school supplies. Now in its third season, Lindor Smile Tuesdays welcomes youth organizations to Citi Field for educational experiences promoting dental health, wellness, self-confidence, and mentorship.
- Growing the Game — Passionate about making baseball accessible and inclusive, Francisco regularly participates in the Mets' Clinic for Champions with Special Olympics Florida and hosts the Lindor Clinic for Kids for local youth leagues and Boys & Girls Clubs."
Lindor is the fifth Mets player to win the award. He joins Curtis Granderson (2016), Carlos Delgado (2006), Al Leiter (2000) and Gary Carter (1989).
The most recent winners of the award are Lindor, Mookie Betts, Salvador Perez, Aaron Judge and Justin Turner over the past five seasons.
The award was originally named the Commissioner's Award when it began in 1971. It was renamed the Roberto Clemente Award just two years later for Clemente, who died on New Year's Eve in 1972 while on a flight delivering supplies to earthquake victims in Nicaragua.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor has won the Roberto Clemente Award from Major League Baseball for his humanitarian work.
Lindor was to receive the award before Game 3 of the World Series on Monday night.
A five-time All-Star, Lindor became the fifth recipient of Puerto Rican descent to receive the award after Edgar Martinez (2004), Carlos Delgado (2006), Carlos Beltrán (2013) and Yadier Molina (2018).
Lindor and his wife Katia have worked with Children’s Miracle Network Hospitals; the SEEN Foundation, a disability advocacy group; Special Olympics Florida; and Boys & Girls Clubs of America.
He donated to relief efforts in Puerto Rico after Hurricanes Maria and Fiona, restoring athletic facilities in his hometown of Caguas, and donated more than $1 million to build Lindor Hall at the Montverde Academy, a school he graduated from in Monteverde, Florida.
Lindor launched a leadership development initiative for students in the sports medicine program at Bayside High School in New York; and funded backpacks and school supplies in Queens, the New York City borough where the Mets' Citi Field is located.
Clemente was a 15-time All-Star from Puerto Rico who was killed in a plane crash on New Year’s Eve 1972 while attempting to deliver supplies to earthquake victims in Nicaragua. The award is given annually to a major league player who represents the sport through character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions on and off the field.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Breaking Down The Strange, Frustrating 2026 Season of Ketel Marte
item.dc:creator: Alex D'Agostino; Unknown
item.description: There's no question about it. The Arizona Diamondbacks did not get the season they might have hoped for out of star second baseman Ketel Marte. But was he really that bad? In some ways, Marte was better than the numbers showed. On the whole, however, it was one of the worse seasons of his lengthy career. item.content:encoded:
There's no question about it. The Arizona Diamondbacks did not get the season they might have hoped for out of star second baseman Ketel Marte.
But was he really that bad?
In some ways, Marte was better than the numbers showed. On the whole, however, it was one of the worse seasons of his lengthy career. And then, of course, there was all the drama from his no-show at Fenway Park.
So let's break it down.
Was Ketel Marte's 2026 season that bad?
In 2026, Marte hit .249/.316/.432 with 2 homers for a .748 OPS. That would generally be considered a productive season for a major league player, but Marte has set a higher standard for himself.
He produced OPS figures of .893, .932 and .843 in his last three seasons, so 2026 was a big step down, close to the levels of his rough 2022 campaign.
Relatively speaking, it wasn't a good year. But the underlying metrics were not poor. His Baseball Savant page is full of red. Marte hit the ball hard. He was well above average in hard-hit rate (43%), average exit velocity (90.2 MPH) and barrel rate (9.4%). His bat speed ticked up to 74.8 MPH, slightly above 2024 and 2025.
His .280 expected batting average was over 30 points higher than his actual average, and ranked in the 90th percentile. By xwOBA (expected weighted on-base average), he placed in the 85th perceentile with a .349.
Marte rarely whiffed (19.7% whiff rate) and struck out at his lowest clip since 2020 (13.7%). He was worth 2.5 WAR by both Baseball Reference and FanGraphs, and played positive second base defense.
And despite an overall lack of situational proudction from the Diamondbacks, Marte had one of the higher RISP averages on the team. He hit .295 with runners in scoring position and .264 with men on. He also provided a pair of dramatic walk-off home runs.
At the same time, Marte's chase rate rose. He chased outside the strike zone just 24.8% of the time in 2025 — a 71st percentile number — but chased 31.5% of the time in 2026.
He swung early in counts and did not put up the same quality of at-bat he has in the past. He walked at his lowest clip since 2021 (8.2%).
And then, of course, there was the drama.
Ketel Marte's inexcused absence
The situation in late August needs little rehashing for those who paid attention, but Marte was unexpectedly absent from a game against the Red Sox on August 17, which led to a restricted list stint with a personal matter cited as the reasoning.
After days of confusion and drama, Marte sat down with his GM, manager and agent at Salt River Fields. It was determined Marte would go on the IL with a knee injury; he'd then apologize to his teammates and rejoin the club.
All of that came to pass. Though there was lingering frustration, especially given the fact it was not the first time Marte had behaved this way, the team and player seemed to move on.
In actuality, Marte played 141 games, the most since 2023. But shifting focus from his play to his behavior was an objectively rough development for both Marte himself and the team.
It's difficult to suggest his season might have played out vastly different had he chosen to show up in Boston. It's possible.
But Marte has always been an emotional player; when things aren't going well, it can be obvious. He's also had excellent overall seasons in years he has been under scrutiny for this type of behavior.
Ultimately, there's no point in continuing to analyze what happened in the past. But the Diamondbacks are going to have to approach Marte a little differently in this regard going forward, and producing on the field will become even more important for the second baseman.
An Arizona native, Alex D'Agostino is the Publisher and credentialed reporter for Arizona Diamondbacks On SI. He previously served as Deputy Editor for Arizona Diamondbacks and Arizona Cardinals On SI and covered both teams for FanSided. Alex also writes for PHNX Sports. Follow Alex on X/Twitter @AlexDagAZ.
Follow alexdagaz

item.title: [MLB.com] Fiery Caminero airs frustrations about Rays' miscues as focus shifts to Game 3
item.dc:creator: Adam Berry
item.description: MILWAUKEE -- Usually, you’ll see Junior Caminero leading with joy. He’s often the first one out of the dugout, celebrating on the field, when one of his teammates has a big moment. He’s quick to rush to their side to provide consolation. He’s even quicker with a big smile and a gleeful shout. item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- Usually, you’ll see Junior Caminero leading with joy. He’s often the first one out of the dugout, celebrating on the field, when one of his teammates has a big moment. He’s quick to rush to their side to provide consolation. He’s even quicker with a big smile and a gleeful shout.
But he showed a different side of his emerging leadership after the sixth inning in Game 2 of the World Series on Saturday night at American Family Field. After seeing the uncharacteristically sloppy Rays blow a four-run lead in an eventual 5-4 loss to the Brewers, Caminero was caught by television cameras shouting at his teammates in the dugout.
“Trying to help the team. Trying to help the team and get our heads up, right?” Caminero said afterward through interpreter Kevin Vera. “Just trying to create some energy and get some life back into us.”
Speaking in front of his locker more than half an hour after Yandy Díaz struck out against Aaron Ashby to end the game, Caminero was clearly still frustrated by his team’s overall performance as the Rays fell into a 2-0 hole.
Asked if he had seen something specific that he didn’t like, leading to his emotional display in the dugout, Caminero responded quickly with a reference to the Rays’ multiple uncharacteristic misplays in the field.
“We had to get outs. In that moment, we weren't doing our job, and against Milwaukee, if you give up outs, they're gonna do that,” Caminero said. “They're gonna use that against you, and that's what happens. So I was trying to say the message [that], 'Hey, we've got to get outs.'”
Caminero also credited the Brewers, acknowledging that the National League champions have “played really well.” And he was optimistic that the Rays would get back to their style of play after being thrust into the World Series spotlight in a raucous environment the past two nights.
“Some players haven't played at this stage, and I understand maybe the pressure that they might feel. Me personally, I've played at similar stages at this point in my career, so I feel comfortable in certain ways,” Caminero said. “We've just got to win. We've just got to do our thing to flip the page, have a fresh mind on Monday and win Game 3.”
Caminero played a part in the Rays’ four-run rally in the first inning, smacking a single to left field that gave them a 2-0 lead, then scoring on Liam Hicks’ two-run homer off Brewers starter Logan Henderson. But Milwaukee kept Tampa Bay’s All-Star third baseman off the basepaths the rest of the night, and the Rays didn’t score again after the first.
That opened the door for the Brewers to come back. So did Tampa Bay’s mistakes on the mound, at the plate, on the bases and in the field.
“That’s the game, right? I guarantee you one thing, that nobody in this clubhouse wants to play the baseball that we've played the last couple days. That's not who we are,” Caminero said. “But at the end of the day, we've played the game in the last two days, and this is the type of baseball that's unfolded. So, it's the game. It's unfortunate.
“We can sit on it tonight, but the rest of the way, it's a new day. It's a new game, and yeah, we look forward to Game 3.”
Caminero had already taken it a step further earlier in his postgame interview, saying the Rays can’t afford to lose another game after the series resumes on Monday night at Tropicana Field.
“They were close, but look, we've got to win,” he said. “The rest of the way, they're mandatory that we've got to win.
“Just go on Monday with a fresh mind, fresh start on Monday and see what happens.”
Caminero attempted to exemplify that as the postgame scrum broke up around his locker, saying, “I already forgot about these last two days. The series now, in my mind, starts on Monday.”
