item.title: [Jays Journal] 3 players the Blue Jays could target if they entertained a Brandon Valenzuela trade
item.dc:creator: Matthew Sookram
item.description: Brandon Valenzuela began the 2026 season as catching depth, but when the season was over he had seemingly solidified himself as the backup catcher for the foreseeable future for the Toronto Blue Jays. What looked like a temporary promotion after Alejandro Kirk fractured his left thumb became a season-long audition in which Valenzuela established himself as an elite defender. He even earned recognition as an American League Gold Glove finalist. That depth is valuable, but it also brings up a legi
item.content:encoded:
Brandon Valenzuela began the 2026 season as catching depth, but when the season was over he had seemingly solidified himself as the backup catcher for the foreseeable future for the Toronto Blue Jays. What looked like a temporary promotion after Alejandro Kirk fractured his left thumb became a season-long audition in which Valenzuela established himself as an elite defender. He even earned recognition as an American League Gold Glove finalist.
That depth is valuable, but it also brings up a legitimate offseason question. With Kirk entrenched as the starter, would the Blue Jays be better served keeping Valenzuela as a high-end backup or using his rising value to address a more pressing need elsewhere on the roster?
Why Valenzuela has real trade value
Valenzuela’s market starts with his defense. In 91 games as a rookie, he ranked among the top five major-league catchers in Statcast Fielding Run Value and FanGraphs’ defensive rating. His framing and blocking gave Toronto’s pitchers a steady target, while his arm helped him throw out 19 of 63 attempted base stealers.
He also held his own at the plate for the first half of the season when he produced a .241/.322/.407 line and a 106 wRC+. Valenzuela’s age and years of club control would certainly be intriguing for prospective teams. Getting a 26-year-old catcher who has already shown he can handle a major-league staff is the type of profile that could be the centre of a decent trade package.
However, there will be detractors around the league. While Valenzuela finished with nine home runs, a double-digit walk rate and a .688 OPS across 271 plate appearances, his second half numbers were not good. He produced a .182/.276/.299 with a 65 wRC+ after the All-Star break. His walk rate held steady, but the strikeouts started to tick up and and he hit just two home runs.
To be fair, rookie catchers often wear down under the physical and mental demands of the position, and teams will likely value his defence first. But it does, limit the return Toronto can reasonably expect. Valenzuela alone is unlikely to fetch an established middle-of-the-order bat or a frontline starter. A more realistic outcome would be a need-for-need deal involving a player with similar control and upside.
What could the Blue Jays get on the trade market for Brandon Valenzuela?
There are several teams that are likely looking for a catcher this offseason and the free agent market is somewhat thin. Three teams that could meet a need-for-need trade are the New York Yankees, Chicago Cubs and Cincinnati Reds.
Yankees - Luis Garcia Jr.
The most ambitious idea would be a deal with the Yankees centred on Luis García Jr. García hit 30 home runs with an .830 OPS in 2026, although his production slipped to a .264/.302/.434 slash line after New York acquired him at the deadline but they are already rumored to be shopping around Garcia this offseason.
His left-handed power would interest Toronto, and returning Garcia back to second base while filling in for Guerrero Jr. at first could address the need to get more pop from the right side of the infield.
The Yankees would almost certainly demand more than Valenzuela in return. But they are also desperate to upgrade on Austin Wells behind the dish and they will need to potentially replace other players such as Trent Grisham, Jazz Chisholm, David Bednar, and Paul Goldschmidt just to name a few.
Cubs - Kevin Alcántara
Chicago is potentially losing Carson Kelly behind the plate, putting the Cubs in need of a replacement. Kevin Alcántara is a 24-year-old right-handed outfielder that will be fighting for playing time with the South Siders. Alcántara hit 20 home runs with an .852 OPS at Triple-A in 2026.
The power and handedness should intrigue Toronto who currently only has two MLB outfielders who bat from the right side and that's Anthony Santander (a switch-hitter and outfielder is a loose term with him) and Davis Schenider (who could be a non-tender candidate).
It could be risky to move a proven MLB backup catcher (at worst) in Valenzuela for Alcántara who has yet to stick around in the big leagues after 37 games over three stints dating back to 2024. But the Blue Jays need some flexibility in their outfield corps and after the Blue Jays had so much success with their last trade with the Cubs they might be wise to go to the well again.
Reds - JJ Bleday
JJ Bleday represents another version of the same need-for-need framework. The Cincinnati outfielder hit .217/.324/.416 with 24 home runs and 72 walks in 2026. Again, the pop is the selling point here and he's under team control through 2028.
His significant second-half drop and stronger production against right-handed pitching make him more of a platoon-oriented corner bat and, as stated, the Blue Jays already have a few of those in Nathan Lukes, Addison Barger, Sean Keys and Yohendrick Piñango. Still, if Cincinnati decides it needs a defensive upgrade behind the plate, Valenzuela could form the foundation of a conversation.
Keeping Valenzuela may still be the better move
The strongest argument against a trade is Kirk’s 2026 injury. Toronto learned how quickly catching depth can derail a season. Valenzuela helped stabilize a key piece of the Blue Jays roster and held his own.
There is also room for both catchers. Kirk is the clear starter, but carrying Valenzuela would allow Toronto to protect him from overuse and they could use either catcher at designated hitter on occasion
Valenzuela has enough value that the Blue Jays should not make him untouchable, and if another club is willing to exchange a controllable everyday outfielder, or a credible second-base option, Toronto would be justified in using its catching depth to improve a thinner area of the roster.
But dealing him simply because Kirk is ahead of him would be a mistake. Valenzuela’s defence, affordability and ability to step into a larger role give the Blue Jays more certainty than most teams possess behind their starting catcher. Unless the return clearly improves the 2027 roster, keeping one of baseball’s better defensive catching tandems is the safer—and probably smarter—choice.

item.title: [inquirer.com] Sorry, Phillies fans, Dave Dombrowski is not going anywhere | Marcus Hayes
item.dc:creator: Marcus Hayes
item.description: Skip to content Sorry, Phillies fans, Dave Dombrowski is not going anywhere for a long, long time. Is that a bad thing? Dealin' Dave, President for Life, denied offering a job to Alex Cora, said Trea Turner must audition at shortstop, and said the farm system is A-OK. Seriously: I hope John Middleton never fires him. If you’re a Dave Dombrowski hater, no matter where you were or what you were doing, your blood ran cold Thursday morning. That was when the Phillies president of baseball operations
item.content:encoded:
Skip to content
Sorry, Phillies fans, Dave Dombrowski is not going anywhere for a long, long time. Is that a bad thing?
Dealin' Dave, President for Life, denied offering a job to Alex Cora, said Trea Turner must audition at shortstop, and said the farm system is A-OK. Seriously: I hope John Middleton never fires him.
If you’re a Dave Dombrowski hater, no matter where you were or what you were doing, your blood ran cold Thursday morning. That was when the Phillies president of baseball operations, in his post-season news conference, blithely remarked:
“I plan on being here for a while. I enjoy it. I’m healthy. I have quality people around me.”
In a town whose football team has lost three straight and whose coach blew the last game in the last 8 seconds; whose basketball team hasn’t gotten past the second round of the playoffs in 25 years; and whose hockey team is winless in its first nine games, Dombrowski is, by far, the most despised sports figure.
And he’s here for the long haul.
Marcus Hayes alerts
During his 61-minute, end-of-season news conference, Dombrowski addressed important issues: Trea Turner’s pending and overdue removal from the shortstop position; his unwillingness to trade from among the starting pitching but his willingness to trade star hitters if those hitters were willing; announcements that Don Mattingly will return as manager and turnover on the coaching staff; and his faith in a minor-league system that he believes is incorrectly rated among the worst in baseball.
But his own future, both long- and short-term, was the most significant issue of the day.
Is that a bad thing? Most Phillies fans, in this moment, would answer, resoundingly, “Yes.”
The backstory
Dombrowski took the Phillies to the World Series in 2022, his second season, but playoff collapses in the following four seasons authored mainly by Dombrowski’s porous bullpens and choking hitters put a target on his back that even José Alvarado could hit. This year, as the Phillies faded from the top wild-card slot to the final wild-card slot to a three-game wild-card exit in Atlanta, Dombrowski’s star sank lower than ever in every corner of Philadelphia ... except one. It’s the only corner that matters.
It’s the office of John Middleton, the Phillies’ managing partner.
Middleton adores Dombrowski. Last month, following up a report by The Athletic that Dombrowski will soon receive an extension beyond his current deal’s expiration in 2027, I was told by a Phillies source, “Middleton will never fire Dombrowski.”
» READ MORE: Don Mattingly ‘carried the stick.’ That helped make him the best choice as Phillies manager.
A few days later, USA Today reported that the Phillies will offer Dombrowski a lifetime contract, presumably to fill whatever role he desires. Right now, at the age of 70, he still desires to decide who’s on the roster and who’s managing them.
Has he earned it? Not in Philadelphia, no. But elsewhere, Dombrowski won two World Series and went to two more. Middleton adores him; essentially, in Middleton’s eyes, Dombrowski can do no wrong.
In my eyes, Dombrowski’s been about average. He inherited an organization that included Bryce Harper, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Aaron Nola, J.T. Realmuto, Alec Bohm, and Bryson Stott.
He’s extended some of those deals, signed Kyle Schwarber (twice), enhanced the roster with trades for Jesús Luzardo and Jhoan Duran, and hit on deadline deals for Harrison Bader in 2025 and Luis Arraez in 2026 (both were hurt in the playoffs, though).
He also has consistently failed to replace the right-handed power of Rhys Hoskins, has shown abominable judgment in bullpen construction, and, in seeking optimal offensive output, has inexcusably and illogically devalued defense, especially for a team so heavily invested in big-money starting pitching: He has four $100 million starters.
Further, the contracts of outfielder Nick Castellanos, a defensive liability, Turner, a defensive liability, and starter Taijuan Walker, the ultimate defensive liability, proved utterly indefensible.
Still, as Middleton loves to point out, any president who takes a team to the playoffs five years in a row must be doing something right.
» READ MORE: To Dave Dombrowski, the Phillies’ problems begin an arm’s length away
Counterpoint: In Dombrowski’s case, so far, most of what he’s done right is that he hasn’t messed with what former GM Matt Klentak left him.
Also: If the Phillies are such a quality team with such a bright future, why did Alex Cora, the manager who won Dombrowski the 2018 World Series in Boston, turn down the manager’s job twice in six months? Does he want to win Puerto Rico the Father of the Year this badly?
Furthermore, if Dombrowski was such a hotshot executive, why did the Sox fire him less than 11 months after winning it all?
None of those questions matter. What matters is, John hearts Dave.
Madness ensues
I, for one, am happy that Dombrowski is sticking around. That’s mainly because I, for one, don’t care if the Phillies win every game, lose every game, or have every game rained out, as long as they’re interesting while doing it.
Also, I enjoy talking to Dombrowski. He’s smart, intriguing, and his hair has its own aura, as the kids say.
Besides, how can I endorse firing a guy who I’m giving a grade like “C?” You know, average. You fire guys who get D’s and F’s.
That “C” grade means Dombrowski probably does a better job at roster building than, say, I, who am a connoisseur of shortstops (and point guards); a far better job than, say Mike Sielski, whose expertise is limited to hockey centermen; but probably not as good a job as David Murphy, who obsesses on wRC+ and FIP (and who, incongruently, is a quarterback aficionado, too).
» READ MORE: Phillies will keep Trea Turner at shortstop for now: ‘He knows he has to be better’
Also, Dombrowski says crazy stuff.
He fired Rob Thomson and, after being turned down by Cora, the fired former Red Sox manager, he replaced Thomson with Mattingly, the bench coach, as interim manager.
Dombrowski said Thursday that, while he’d followed a baseball mandate and interviewed other candidates, he had never offered the job to anyone but Mattingly. He said this with a straight face ... after both USA Today and the Phillies’ own website reported that, early last week, Cora had turned him down again.
Dombrowski on Thursday also said he actually signed Mattingly to a deal last Saturday, but, with the Eagles playing Sunday (24 hours later) and with Mattingly lacking solid internet service at his vacation lodgings, they delayed leaking the news until Wednesday ... so as to have better Wi-Fi on Thursday for Mattingly’s Zoom news conference.
I am not making any of that up.
Old MacDonald’s farm
Dombrowski also tried to convince listeners that their farm system is better than the experts rank it, which is generally between fifth-to-last and second-to-last. He asserted that major league rookies Andrew Painter, Justin Crawford, and Alex McFarlane should count toward their farm depth, and that they should be credited for using prospects to acquire Luzardo and Duran.
Dombrowski ignored the fact that Painter and Crawford did not factor into the current rankings at all, and he ignored the fact that teams ranked higher than his also traded prospects to improve. For instance, the Dodgers traded three prospects at the deadline to acquire Tarik Skubal from the Tigers, two of them ranked in the top 100 by MLB.com, and still had an elite system at the season’s end. The Brewers also traded prospects for bullpen help at the deadline, and their farm system remains as good or better than the Dodgers’ — whom they just swept out of the NLCS.
Coup de grace
The nuttiest thing Dombrowski said in his hourlong State of the Union regarded Turner. By most metrics, Turner was, by far, the worst defensive shortstop in all of baseball. Dombrowski’s solution:
He forced Turner to leave his home in Florida and travel to Philadelphia for a two-hour meeting with Dombrowski, which is like a kid on summer break getting called back to school to go to the principal’s office. What did they talk about for two hours? Some of it concerned Turner’s career-worst offensive performance, which is weird, since that’s kind of the job of the manager and the hitting coach. Some of it concerned Turner’s defense.
Dombrowski warned Turner that Turner would have to audition in spring training if he hopes to retain the shortstop job. Otherwise, he will be moved, most likely to left field, though Turner would prefer staying on the infield, most likely at second base.
» READ MORE: The most imaginative changes the Phillies can make begin with moving Trea Turner off shortstop
What?
WHAT?
So, the plan to return the 33-year-old’s defensive skills from putridity back to their heights, which were mediocrity, is to have him walk on eggshells for 20 spring training games? In which he will play, what, a total of 90 innings — 90 innings that Turner could spend acclimating himself to second base, where he’s started just 79 games, or left field where he’s played zero games?
Assume Turner exits spring training as the shortstop, then he commits four errors in April — again. Do you banish him to the grass or push him to the right side of the infield in the middle of the season? What chance does he have to succeed in that sort of atmosphere?
Of all the harebrained schemes the Phillies have hatched in the past 15 years or so, the plan for Turner is the wildest. Really, this stuff just writes itself. Thanks, Dave.
And, Mr. Middleton: To hell with your fans. For my sake, and for the sake of columnists everywhere, please never fire Dave Dombrowski.

item.title: [puckettspond.com] This year's World Series shows where the Twins have failed
item.dc:creator: Chris Schad
item.description: The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful. Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a s
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful.
Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a sweep over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night and they will face either the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians in what will be a showdown between small-market teams.
While this year’s matchup could create a loophole for the Pohlad family to avoid dropping a large amount of money to improve the team, it also reflects poorly on their decisions that have kept them from competing over the past few years.
The Brewers, Rays and Guardians are showing the Twins how to build a winner
As you may have guessed, the Brewers, Guardians and Rays are not among MLB’s biggest spenders. According to Cot’s Baseball Contracts, the Brewers’ year-end salary ranked 23rd at $99.3 million and defeated the Dodgers’ No. 1 roster at $366.0 million. The American League finalists were also budget-conscious as the Rays ranked 20th with a year-end payroll of $103.1 million and the Guardians ranked 25th at $91.0 million.
All three of the remaining teams had a lower year-end payroll than the Twins, who ranked 17th with a figure of $123.9 million and while many, including owner and chairman Tom Pohlad, believe that adding to that number could lead to a championship, the other three teams show what they have done wrong.
The first is maximizing the value of players on the roster. The Rays, Guardians and Brewers have traded players before they get to free agency to add to their organization and it’s paid off in a big way. The Brewers most notably did this in a February 2024 trade featuring Corbin Burnes that brought back left-hander DL Hall and infielder Joey Ortiz.
The Rays also have done this with their trade of Triple-A right-hander Tobias Myers, who was traded to Cleveland as he was eligible for the Rule 5 Draft in 2021, and brought back star third baseman Junior Caminero in return. While the Guardians whiffed on Myers, they made other shrewd deals that netted them Craig Yoho, Patrick Bailey, Foster Griffin and Kyle Manzardo.
These trades are a double-edged sword as they usually involve popular players. But it brings back pieces that ensure a larger championship window. That leaves player development as the final phase of the three contenders and each team has a homegrown star to lean on such as Jose Ramirez, Jacob Misiorowski or Caminero.
The Twins’ biggest problems go beyond their payroll
Turning the attention back to the Twins, it’s easy to see where they have come up short. This year’s trade deadline was one opportunity to shift the narrative. But instead of trading players that could bring back a big return such as Ryan Jeffers and Joe Ryan, the Twins went the opposite direction, adding A.J. Minter, Jeff Hoffman and Dean Kremer.
Even when they tried to trade Trevor Larnach to the Houston Astros before owner Jim Crane vetoed it, they were seeking 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, a pitcher who posted his highest ERA (3.73) and lowest WAR (1.0) since his rookie season in 2021.
The other key issue is the Twins’ player development. While top prospects such as Royce Lewis and Matt Wallner thrive initially when reaching the major leagues, those players have hit a wall when pitchers adjust to them. The problem can be traced back to Miguel Sano’s downfall in the early 2020s and can still be seen in a group of post-hype hitters that haven’t lived up to their prospect status.
This leaves the Twins in a tricky spot this offseason. After failing to trade Jeffers at the deadline, there’s a good chance he’ll leave in free agency. Ryan has a year of team control remaining, but trading him now could get a pair of MLB-ready players in return. Several top prospects including Walker Jenkins, Emmanuel Rodriguez and Kaelen Culpepper made their debuts this season, but the key will be to make sure they don’t regress entering their first full season in the bigs.
Of course, fans may cheer for a salary floor to hold the Pohlads accountable for what happens to the Twins next. But the Rays, Guardians and Brewers show that paying top dollar may not be necessary to build a contender and Minnesota would be wise to follow their blueprint.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Rays Need Junior Caminero to Wake Up Before It's Too Late
item.dc:creator: Christian Rauh
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays are now facing a difficult situation in the American League Championship Series after falling 3-2 to the Cleveland Guardians in Game 3 on Thursday. And while there are plenty of things to criticize about the performance, I think the biggest concern continues to be the lack of offensive production from Tampa Bay's biggest stars. Especially Junior Caminero. The Rays' star slugger had arguably his worst performance of the season against Cleveland, going 0-for-4 with four strikeou
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are now facing a difficult situation in the American League Championship Series after falling 3-2 to the Cleveland Guardians in Game 3 on Thursday.
And while there are plenty of things to criticize about the performance, I think the biggest concern continues to be the lack of offensive production from Tampa Bay's biggest stars.
Especially Junior Caminero.
The Rays' star slugger had arguably his worst performance of the season against Cleveland, going 0-for-4 with four strikeouts.
And it wasn't necessarily because Gavin Williams was throwing pitches that were impossible to hit. Caminero consistently took hittable pitches early in counts before chasing balls well outside the strike zone.
That's something we haven't seen much of throughout the regular season. A year where he has surely earned votes for American League MVP.
And I think it's fair to wonder whether Caminero is trying to do too much at the plate.
The 45-home-run slugger still hasn't hit a home run this postseason, and his batting average sits at .238 with a .666 OPS.
Those numbers certainly aren't what Tampa Bay needs from one of its biggest offensive weapons.
But Caminero isn't the only player struggling.
Yandy Díaz is hitting .240 with a .589 OPS, while Jonathan Aranda has managed just a .182 batting average and .568 OPS.
Victor Mesa Jr. is hitting .143, and Liam Hicks isn't doing much better at .167.
These are supposed to be the players carrying Tampa Bay's offense.
Instead, the Rays have relied on contributions from the bottom of their lineup.
Chandler Simpson delivered Tampa Bay's only two runs Thursday with an impressive two-RBI triple against Williams.
Richie Palacios has also provided some important hits, while Jonny DeLuca has been one of Tampa Bay's more productive hitters throughout the series.
But that can't continue being the expectation.
Tampa Bay won 98 games during the regular season because it had a lineup capable of consistently putting the baseball in play and creating scoring opportunities.
However, the Rays have yet to score more than four runs in a postseason game.
And Thursday might've been the most frustrating example.
Tampa Bay managed just three hits and struck out 13 times, including seven strikeouts from the top of the batting order.
The Rays also went down in order in seven of their nine offensive innings.
That's not going to get the job done in October.
Especially against a Cleveland team that has consistently taken advantage of its opportunities.
Now, I'm not suggesting Tampa Bay's season is over.
The Rays are only trailing 2-1 in a seven-game series, and there's still plenty of baseball left to play.
But if Tampa Bay wants to reach the World Series, its biggest offensive stars need to start playing like it.
And that starts with Junior Caminero.

New York entered the playoffs as the No. 4 seed after finishing the regular seas
item.content:encoded:
New York radio host Tommy Lugauer has made a strong case for the New York Yankees to pursue San Diego Padres star Fernando Tatis Jr. in a blockbuster trade. Lugauer argued that the outfielder could address several of the team's roster concerns.
The Yankees' 2026 postseason campaign ended with a 3-0 sweep by the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series, extending their World Series drought to 17 seasons. New York entered the playoffs as the No. 4 seed after finishing the regular season with a 93-68 record, second in the AL East behind Tampa Bay.
Following the disappointing postseason exit, Lugauer discussed the Yankees' offseason priorities during a segment on WFAN Sports Radio. He argued that acquiring the $340 million star should be at the top of the team's list, praising the 27-year-old's offensive production, defensive ability, and potential fit in New York.
"The Yankees' top priority in the offseason should be doing everything in their power to acquire Fernando Tatis Jr. Tatis would solve a million issues for the Yankees. Leadoff hitter clutch, an electric player defensively, offensively. I think Fernando Tatis Junior would be a rock star in New York, a rock star. And he should be their future right fielder for the Yankees," said Lugauer.
He added:
"Judge is to either DH or first base, and or maybe a combination of both. Right field's going to be wide open, and who better to man right field for years to come with the Yankees than Tatis?"
Fernando Tatis last played in the 2026 postseason on October 7, when the Padres lost 3-1 to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the National League Division Series, ending San Diego's season.
Fernando Tatis Jr. reflects on the Padres' 2026 season
After the San Diego Padres lost to the Milwaukee Brewers in Game 4 of the NLDS and got eliminated from the playoffs, Fernando Tatis Jr. spoke to reporters about what he had learned throughout the season and his determination to keep improving.
The outfielder emphasized his commitment to growing both on and off the field, while continuing to work toward delivering the results San Diego's fans expect.
"It's a lot of learning experience. I was just gonna put it that way, you know, this game will teach you so many stuff on and off the field every single year, so at my disposal. Simple servant, I'm just here to keep learning every single year to keep getting better as a person, as a man. As a father, you know, and we're just gonna keep battling and find a way to give San Diego what they really deserve," said Tatis.
Fernando Tatis finished the 2026 regular season with 181 hits and 96 runs scored across 159 games, recording 626 at-bats.

item.title: [mlb.com] Who should Brewers want to face in the World Series?
item.dc:creator: Zach Sweet
item.description: When the Brewers finished off the Dodgers on Thursday night, their World Series opponent was the last thing on anyone’s mind. An MLB official closed the postgame press conference by telling manager Pat Murphy and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, “We’ll see you in Milwaukee at the World Series.” Murphy’s reply said everything: “When’s that start?” Next Friday, Oct. 23, at American Family Field, where Milwaukee holds home-field advantage thanks to its franchise-record 103 wins. The Guardians took a 2-1 ALCS
item.content:encoded:
When the Brewers finished off the Dodgers on Thursday night, their World Series opponent was the last thing on anyone’s mind. An MLB official closed the postgame press conference by telling manager Pat Murphy and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, “We’ll see you in Milwaukee at the World Series.”
Murphy’s reply said everything: “When’s that start?”
Next Friday, Oct. 23, at American Family Field, where Milwaukee holds home-field advantage thanks to its franchise-record 103 wins. The Guardians took a 2-1 ALCS lead over the Rays into Friday night's scheduled Game 4 at Progressive Field. Milwaukee, meanwhile, will have a full week to rest, which leaves plenty of time to watch and wonder.
Here’s a guide to each potential matchup. You decide which one you’d rather see.
If the regular season is a guide ...
It doesn’t tell us much. The Brewers went 2-1 against both teams.
Milwaukee won the first two games against Cleveland on June 16-17 before rookie left-hander Parker Messick struck out nine over six innings in the finale. Cleveland was without José Ramírez, Angel Martínez and Chase DeLauter. All three are back.
When the Brewers hit
Milwaukee’s lineup is built on pressure. The Brewers ranked in the top five in doubles, runs, hits, walks, batting average and on-base percentage.
That approach might get more of a test against Tampa Bay. The Rays issued the fewest walks in the Majors (409) and ranked second in defensive runs saved (87). Drawing walks and finding holes gets tougher against that combination. And their top starters have carried it into October: Drew Rasmussen has a 1.29 ERA through two postseason starts, while Peralta has allowed one earned run in 10 2/3 innings, including six shutout innings in Game 2 of the ALCS.
Cleveland offers a different challenge. Gavin Williams has been a monster, striking out 33 over 16 2/3 innings this postseason. The Guardians have a 2.54 ERA this October, slightly better than Tampa Bay’s 2.72. But Cleveland issued 530 regular-season walks to the Rays’ 409, giving Milwaukee more reason to believe its patient approach can create traffic.
When the other side hits
The regular-season numbers favor facing Cleveland. The Guardians had the lowest OPS (.696) and fewest runs (678) of any postseason team. Tampa Bay offered a more complete attack, with Junior Caminero’s 42 homers anchoring a lineup that tied for fifth in on-base percentage (.326).
October has told a different story. Through Thursday, Cleveland was averaging 4.25 runs per game with a .685 OPS, compared with Tampa Bay’s 3.00 runs and .563 OPS. The Guardians haven’t suddenly become an offensive powerhouse, but they’ve been more productive than the Rays, whose lineup managed just three hits in Game 3 of the ALCS.
The larger sample still points toward Cleveland as the preferable opponent. The way these teams are hitting right now makes that a tougher call.
The bullpens
Neither ninth inning looks inviting. Tampa Bay’s Bryan Baker has saved all four Rays wins this postseason without allowing a hit in four innings. Ian Seymour has been a strong bridge, allowing one earned run in 6 1/3 innings.
Cleveland counters with Cade Smith, who has allowed two hits and one run while striking out 13 in nine innings this October. Hunter Gaddis has added six scoreless innings across seven appearances. Both teams have arms capable of shortening games.
The Brewers have made a habit of coming back this postseason, and their bats have shown they can pick at a bullpen late. Against either opponent, getting a lead before the closer enters would make life easier.
What about the intangibles?
The Guardians’ championship drought dates to 1948. The Rays, like the Brewers, have never won a World Series.
The Rays mirror Milwaukee in many ways. Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold worked in Tampa Bay’s front office alongside current Rays GM Erik Neander. Add Peralta facing his former team, and the storyline writes itself.
Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt played for Milwaukee and interviewed for the job that went to Murphy three years ago. And a Cleveland-Milwaukee World Series comes with a built-in movie reference: Major League, filmed in Milwaukee with Bob Uecker’s Harry Doyle calling Cleveland's improbable run.
The verdict
Give the Guardians a slight edge as Milwaukee’s preferred opponent, though their October bats have made that a tougher sell. The Rays were the more complete team over six months. Cleveland has spent the past two weeks making those six months feel a little less relevant.
The Brewers? They just sent the back-to-back champs home. They’ll let the AL sort this out. Somebody remind Murph what time Friday’s game starts.

item.title: [mlb.com] Mitchell keeps proving doubters wrong -- all the way to the World Series
item.dc:creator: Adam McCalvy
item.description: Ever since, there have been people who doubted that Mitchell could stay healthy enough, long enough, to handle the rigors of center field for a season that stretches 162 games, and, for the pennant-winning Brewers, well beyond. But he’s played more games this year than his first four years combined, and he was plenty healthy enough on Thursday night to deliver the tiebreaking solo home run that sent the Brewers from four runs down in the early innings to a victory and a trip to the World Series.
item.content:encoded:
Ever since, there have been people who doubted that Mitchell could stay healthy enough, long enough, to handle the rigors of center field for a season that stretches 162 games, and, for the pennant-winning Brewers, well beyond. But he’s played more games this year than his first four years combined, and he was plenty healthy enough on Thursday night to deliver the tiebreaking solo home run that sent the Brewers from four runs down in the early innings to a victory and a trip to the World Series.
“Growing up, he’s always one that his chip, his edge, his grit, was proving people wrong,” said Antony Mitchell, Garrett’s dad. “I told him, ‘It’s time to make the big shift.' That’s what he’s doing right now.”
Mitchell had two hits in the NLCS, a 4-0 Brewers sweep of the two-time defending World Series champion Dodgers. He made them count. In Game 3 on Wednesday, he followed Jake Bauers’ go-ahead, 11-pitch, two-run homer with a solo shot for the third set of back-to-back homers for left-handed hitters off a left-handed pitcher in postseason history. Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig were the first in 1928. Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper were the second earlier this month.
A night later, Mitchell connected off a lefty again. The Brewers had trailed, 4-0, after slumping superstar Shohei Ohtani came to life with a three-run home run. No team had ever come back from a deficit that large to complete a postseason series sweep. Until these Brewers.
In the sixth, the Dodgers brought in a fresh left-handed reliever in Tanner Scott. He had not allowed a home run to a left-handed hitter all year, regular season and postseason. At the bat rack, right-handed hitter Andrew Vaughn stood ready to pinch-hit if called upon.
“I just heard an explosion go off,” Vaughn said. “The ball was crushed. What a sweet swing.”
Naturally, Mitchell said he was just trying to have a good at-bat, especially after falling behind, 0-2. He looked at three straight balls out of the strike zone, then got a fastball as center-cut as they come. Mitchell hit it out. The Brewers had the lead. For the sixth time in their seven victories in eight games so far this postseason, they came from behind to win.
“We’re savages, man,” Mitchell said. “We go down four runs early there, and nobody panics. This is what we’ve been doing. I’m just so proud of our team.”
Imagine how proud dad was, up in the stands. He could tell the game was slowing down for his son by the way he carried himself, pitch to pitch. And how proud the Brewers’ amateur scouting director, Tod Johnson, was feeling as he watched it unfold.
“I’ll be honest: He’s probably not a Brewer if he doesn’t have diabetes,” Johnson said. “He fell [to 20th overall] because of concerns about that. Then he battled through different injuries that are not necessarily related to that. But [before the Draft], we did a lot of work on it.”
It helped that Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold had history with Rays outfielder Sam Fuld, a diabetic and one of Mitchell’s role models as a young ballplayer.
“To do something like he did on this stage is a message for everybody that if you put your mind to it, you can do it,” Arnold said. “He’s overcome so much.”
They all know well what it took Mitchell to get to that moment. He wears a pod that delivers insulin and is connected to his cell phone, which Mitchell checks periodically throughout the day and during games. On several occasions this season, Mitchell’s blood sugar got out of whack and he had to miss games. With his increased workload, he had to train himself to eat more, and at the right times, to be available as often as possible.
Along the way, he has met many young diabetic kids playing sports, offering advice and support.
“He has managed himself for many years, and here he is, an example to kids that anything is possible,” Antony Mitchell said. “It’s a disease, and you have to learn to manage it. It’s not easy. He makes things look easy sometimes, but he works really hard to make it all work. These were special moments.
“He loves kids, he loves this game, he loves his team. Here they are, celebrating. We’re going to the World Series. This is so fantastic.”

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] The Season That Was: Kevin Gausman
item.dc:creator: Tom Dakers
item.description: 2026 was the final season of Kevin Gausman's five-year, $110 million free-agent contract. In the first four seasons, Kevin posted a 48-41 record, a 3.48 ERA, and an 11.5 bWAR. A good return on a big free-agent contract. Not all that many of those go as well as this one did. But 2026 was his age-35 season, and sometimes pitchers don't do well in their mid-30s. | Age | Team | WAR | W | L | ERA | G | GS | IP | H | R | ER | HR | BB | IBB | SO | HBP | BK | WP | BF | ERA+ | FIP | | 35 | 2TM | 1.1 | 9
item.content:encoded:
2026 was the final season of Kevin Gausman's five-year, $110 million free-agent contract. In the first four seasons, Kevin posted a 48-41 record, a 3.48 ERA, and an 11.5 bWAR. A good return on a big free-agent contract. Not all that many of those go as well as this one did.
But 2026 was his age-35 season, and sometimes pitchers don't do well in their mid-30s.
| Age | Team | WAR | W | L | ERA | G | GS | IP | H | R | ER | HR | BB | IBB | SO | HBP | BK | WP | BF | ERA+ | FIP |
| 35 | 2TM | 1.1 | 9 | 12 | 4.51 | 32 | 32 | 177.2 | 179 | 96 | 89 | 26 | 47 | 1 | 184 | 1 | 3 | 2 | 750 | 97 | 3.74 |
| 35 | TOR | 1.0 | 5 | 10 | 4.38 | 23 | 23 | 127.1 | 128 | 68 | 62 | 15 | 36 | 1 | 127 | 1 | 3 | 1 | 540 | 101 | 3.51 |
| 35 | CHC | 0.1 | 4 | 2 | 4.83 | 9 | 9 | 50.1 | 51 | 28 | 27 | 11 | 11 | 0 | 57 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 210 | 88 | 4.33 |
Provided by Baseball-Reference.com: View Original Table
Generated 10/15/2026.
Baseball Reference has him at a 1.1 WAR (down from 4.0). FanGraphs 3.1 (down from 4.1), giving him a value of $25.1 million to the Jays and Cubs.
He had a 3.3.74 FIP and a 3.58 xFIP, which is why the FanGraphs WAR is so much better than the Baseball Reference one.
Kevin's BABIP was .311 (up from.262 last year). 68.7% of his base runner were stranded (down from 72.2%).
His line drive rate was down a little bit (19.6% from 21.3 last year), ground ball rate up (40.3% down from 36.7), and fly ball rate much the same (40.3% from 42.0). 12.7% of fly balls hit off him left the park, up from 9.5.
His strikeout rate about the same (24.5% from 24.4), and his walk rate was down a bit (6.3% from 6.5).
Kevin's soft contact was up (17.4% from 15.1 last year) and hard contact about the same (35.9% from 36.2).
He was better against LHB (.251/.304/.389) than RHB (.269/.307/.459). He's been slightly better against LHB for his career.
He was better at home (3.83 ERA, batters hit .264/.299/.439) than on the road (5.40, .253/.313/.394).
Kevin was better in the first half of the season (4.33, .244/.296/.405) than the second half (4.82, .284/.320/.444).
Gausman by month:
- April: 7 starts, 2-2, 3.10. Batters hit .204/.244/.349, 5 home runs, 8 walks and 40 strikeouts.
- May: 5 starts, 2-1, 3.18. Batters hit .291/.316/.364, 1 home run, 4 walks and 26 strikeouts.
- June: 6 starts, 0-4, 6.47. Batters hit .262/.324/.556, 9 home runs, 12 walks and 34 strikeouts.
- July: 4 starts, 0-3, 6.10. Batters hit .280/.366/.317, 3 home runs, 11 walks and 23 strikeouts.
- August: 6 starts, 4-1, 4.54. Batters hit .275/.312/.443, 5 home runs, 8 walks and 33 strikeouts.
- September: 4 starts, 1-1, 4.43. Batters hit .267/.298/.478, 6 home runs, 4 walks and 28 strikeouts.
The Jays were 9-14 in his starts. The Cubs were 5-4 in his starts. Between the two teams, they averaged 4.05 runs scored in games he started. They scored 2 or less runs in 13 of his starts.
Days of rest:
- 4 days, 12 games: 3.54, .246/.288/.404.
- 5 days, 16 games: 5.26, .265/.313/.433.
- 6 or more days, 4 games: 4.50, .275/.326/.413
I love guys who are best on normal rest. I think we are all creatures of habit, you get in a routine and things go well, you leave that routine and they don't got as well. He was also best on normal rest last year.
Times through the order:
- 1st: Batters hit .233/.276/.346.
- 2nd: Batters hit .270/.318/.460.
- 3rd: Batters hit .286/.333/.478.
- And he faced 1 batter a fourth time, getting the out.
I wonder if he would consider being a reliever next year? That might be reading too much into one season, in 2025 he was pretty much the same for each of the first three times through the order.
By Catcher:
- Brandon Valenzuela: 4.46, .254/.298/.396 in 308 PA.
- Alejandro Kirk: 4.81, .263/.324/.419 in 185 PA.
- Carson Kelly: 4.20, .226/.268/.426 in 123 PA.
- Miguel Amaya: 5.75, .305/.333/.500 in 87 PA.
- Tyler Heineman: 2.31, .273/.319/.409 in 47 PA.
Kevin's best start, by GameScore, was a 78 on April 1st, at home against the Rockies. He went 6 innings, 2 hits, 0 earned runs, 0 walks, and 10 strikeouts. He also had a 77 and two 76s.
Worst start? A 13 in Chicago against the Cubs, on June 19th. You likely remember it: 2 innings, 7 hits, 7 earned runs, 1 home run, 4 walks and 3 strikeouts. We used six relievers, two days after a bullpen day, and the next day Patrick Corbin was pulled after 3.2 innings.
Kevin averaged 5.5 innings per start in his 23 starts with us. And about the same in his 9 starts with the Cubs. His one playoff start didn't go all that well: 3.1 innings, 3 earned.
He threw, for the most part, three pitches:
- Four Seamer: 93.8 mph (last year it averaged 94.5). Batters hit .289 against it (.230 last year).
- Split finger: 84 mph (last year it averaged 94.9). Batters hit .207 against it (.191 last year).
- Slider: 84.1 mph (last year it averaged 83.2). Batters hit .324 against it (.333 last year).
Random Baseball Savant numbers:
- Fastball Run Value: 87th percentile.
- Breaking Ball Run Value: 7th percentile.
- Chase Rate: 88th percentile.
- Strikeout %: 70th percentile.
- Walk %: 86th percentile.
- Barrell %: 46th percentile.
- Hard Hit %: 34th percentile.
- Expected ERA: 53rd percentile.
With the Jays, he posted a 53-51 record and a 3.63 ERA, with a 12.5 bWAR (and a 21 fWAR). FanGraphs says he was worth $167.6 million over his five-year contract, and he was paid $110 million, so we got more than our money's worth.
On the Jays career leaderboard:
- 11th in pitcher bWAR: 12.5.
- 7th in ERA: 3.62
- 11th in wins: 53 (tied with Jose Berrios)
- 11th in innings pitched: 861.0.
- 7th in strikeouts: 920.
- 9th in games started: 148.
He also started 7 playoff games (and pitched once in relief) for the Jays. He had a 3.79 ERA and a 2-4 record.
The last I saw, Gausman was talking about retirement, but he has said that he would consider coming back to the Jays. As I mentioned above, he was terrific the first time through the order, and far less good the second and third times. But I'm not sure that he would want to come back to pitch out of the pen.
The trade looks very good for the Jays, Brett Bateman was terrific for us, in his 41 games. Ty Southisene played well for 11 games with Vancouver, hitting .262/.380/.429. It will be interesting to watch how he does. FanGraphs had him listed as the Cubs 27th best prospect. He's fast and plays good defense in the middle of the infield.
It was great getting to watch Gausman pitch. The last five seasons wouldn't have been nearly as much fun without him.

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies were eliminated from the MLB playoffs in the National League Wild Card Round.
The Atlanta Braves beat the Phillies 2-1 in the Wild Card Series at Truist Park.
The Braves have since been eliminated. Currently the Milwaukee Brewers hold a 3-0 lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series, and the Cleveland Guardians hold a 2-1 lead over the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Championship Series.
Amid the ALCS and NLCS, Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski met with the media. During the session, Dombrowski announced news involving Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber.
Philadelphia Phillies Announce Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber Updates After Playoff Elimination
ATLANTA, GEORGIA – SEPTEMBER 30: Kyle Schwarber #12 of the Philadelphia Phillies celebrates a home run with Bryce Harper #3 of the Philadelphia Phillies against the Atlanta Braves during the eighth inning in game two of the National League Wild Card Series at Truist Park on September 30, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)
Dombrowski said that Harper will be the full-time first baseman in 2027, according to Justin Heinze of Patch.com.
The Phillies’ POBO also said that Schwarber is expected to get more reps at first base to help manage Harper’s workload.
PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA – MAY 06: Bryce Harper #3 high fives Kyle Schwarber #12 of the Philadelphia Phillies after a run in the eighth inning against the Athletics at Citizens Bank Park on May 06, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images)
Harper began the 2026 season as the Phillies’ starting first baseman.
However, the Phillies had Harper play some right field, his old position, after they acquired second baseman Luis Arraez at the trade deadline.
SEATTLE, WASHINGTON – AUGUST 25: Bryce Harper #3 of the Philadelphia Phillies makes a catch for an out during the eighth inning against the Seattle Mariners at T-Mobile Park on August 25, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images)
Acquiring Arraez led to Bryson Stott moving to third base and Alec Bohm taking more reps at first base.
The Arraez acquisition also led to Schwarber getting some reps at first base. The primary DH appeared in eight games at DH this past season. He also appeared in two games at left field.
Looking at Bryce Harper’s 2026 Season
NEW YORK, NEW YORK – JUNE 27: Bryce Harper #3 of the Philadelphia Phillies catches a throw to first during the first inning against the New York Mets at Citi Field on June 27, 2026 in New York City. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)
Harper posted 3.3 fWAR and a .269/.380/.485 (135 wRC+) slash line with 29 home runs and 87 RBI over 162 games in 2026.
Defensively, Harper posted 0 Defensive Runs Saved and -5 Outs Above Average over 923 2/3 innings at first base. In right field, Harper recorded -5 DRS and -3 OAA over 363 2/3 innings.
Harper went 3-for-13 with a home run and a double in the Wild Card Series against Atlanta.
Looking at Kyle Schwarber’s 2026 Season
ATLANTA, GEORGIA – OCTOBER 01: Kyle Schwarber #12 of the Philadelphia Phillies walks to first base against the Atlanta Braves during the fourth inning in game three of the National League Wild Card Series at Truist Park on October 01, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)
Schwarber posted 2.9 fWAR and a .232/.354/.503 (130 wRC+) slash line with 45 home runs and 97 RBI over 156 regular-season games in 2026.
During the Wild Card Series, Schwarber went 4-for-11 with a home run and two walks.

item.title: [MLB.com] LIVE: Brewers-Dodgers NLCS Game 4 (FS1/FOX One)
item.dc:creator: Sonja Chen; Adam McCalvy; AJ Cassavell
item.description: Milwaukee brings a commanding 3-0 lead into Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. But the Dodgers are the champs until they’re not, and they’ve faced plenty of adversity on their way to World Series titles in each of the past two seasons. Never like this though. item.content:encoded:
Milwaukee brings a commanding 3-0 lead into Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Thursday night. But the Dodgers are the champs until they’re not, and they’ve faced plenty of adversity on their way to World Series titles in each of the past two seasons.
Never like this though. In all best-of-seven postseason series, teams with a 3-0 lead have gone on to win that series 41 times out of 42 -- with 32 of those series ending as sweeps. Only two teams have ever even forced a Game 7 after trailing 3-0, and only the 2004 Red Sox, in the ALCS against the Yankees, have come all the way back to win.
“It's certainly possible,” said Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, himself a fabled part of that Red Sox rally. “I've lived it. And I think the thing is that our guys have been battle-tested. … It's an elimination game. We've played in a lot of elimination games. We've just got to get a win.”
While the Dodgers chase baseball history, the Brewers can make a bit of their own with a win on Thursday. A year ago, they were swept by the Dodgers in the very same round. If they can return the favor, they would become the first team to be swept out of the playoffs, only to sweep the same team -- in any postseason series -- a year later. But they’re not getting ahead of themselves.
“We have yet to complete anything,” Brewers outfielder Jackson Chourio said through an interpreter. “The job's not finished for us. So we have to come with the same mentality. Which is to win.”
Here’s what you need to know about Game 4:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 4 is currently airing nationally on FS1.
All series are available in the US on MLB.TV with authentication to a participating Pay TV provider. Games also are available live internationally, although not in Canada. Sportsnet is MLB's exclusive English language broadcaster in Canada for every Postseason game, while TVA Sports will be covering the entire AL Postseason and the World Series in French and Broadcaster RDS will cover the entire NL Postseason in French.
The Brewers picked Drohan from among a plethora of fresh options to start what amounts to a bullpen game. Left-handers Kyle Harrison and Drohan and right-hander Chad Patrick have been on the roster for both the NLDS and NLCS, but have yet to pitch in any of the Brewers’ first seven games. Midseason pickup Dustin May, the former Dodger who won a World Series ring with L.A. in 2020, pitched an inning in NLCS Game 2 on what would have been a bullpen day had he been lined up to start Thursday. They are all options to come in behind Drohan, who had a 4.19 ERA in 33 games/19 starts and shifted to the bullpen late in the season when he came upon a loose innings limit. He thrived in short stints, posting a 1.47 ERA as a reliever. It will be his career postseason debut.
The Dodgers' 7-0 postseason record when Glasnow pitches is more of a quirk than anything else, but the right-hander has gotten the results to back it up. In four starts and three relief appearances, Glasnow has recorded a 1.73 ERA (five earned runs in 26 innings). Glasnow had command issues when he last pitched against the Braves in NLDS Game 4 -- issuing five walks -- but limited the damage to one run in 4 2/3 innings.
What are the starting lineups?
Brewers: The lineup the Brewers used against right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto in Game 2 produced the second postseason game in franchise history in which five different players tallied multiple hits. Against Glasnow in Game 4, they hope for a similar result with the same group.
Dodgers: Not only are the Dodgers sticking with Shohei Ohtani despite his lingering right biceps and left knee issues, they're bumping him up to leadoff for a must-win game. He and a scuffling Will Smith -- batting cleanup for Game 4 -- were dropped in the lineup in the past couple games, but the fact that both contributed to L.A.'s lone run-scoring rally in Game 3 likely played a role in Roberts' decision to elevate them Thursday.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Brewers: Right-handed setup man Abner Uribe, who has appeared in each of the first seven games of the postseason, finally wilted a bit in Game 3, walking three batters ahead of Smith’s two-run double in the sixth inning. But left-hander DL Hall kept the game on track by stopping the rally there and recording seven enormous outs. Then Trevor Megill logged a four-out save. That’s a lot of work for those last two arms, so lefty Aaron Ashby figures to play a prominent role in Game 4 if the score is tight.
Dodgers: It's all hands on deck, with the possible exception of Justin Wrobleski, who threw 32 pitches to cover the final 1 2/3 innings of Game 3. Roberts made a point of saying that he will get closer Edwin Díaz --- the only Dodgers reliever who has not pitched this series -- into Game 4.
Any injuries of note?
Brewers: None.
Dodgers: Ohtani (right biceps, left knee) and Freeman (right knee) are managing lingering injuries. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option. Blake Treinen (right shoulder inflammation) is unlikely to pitch this postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Brewers: Chourio’s .642 OPS in this postseason doesn’t tell anything about his impact. His leadoff home run in Game 3 marked his second homer of the 2026 postseason and sixth of his career, breaking a brief tie with William Contreras for the most homers in Brewers’ postseason history. Three of them have led off a postseason game, which matched Hall of Famer Derek Jeter, Jimmy Rollins and Ohtani for the second-most in history, trailing only Kyle Schwarber, who has five leadoff home runs in the postseason. And with his 18th career postseason RBI, Chourio also broke a tie with Hall of Famer Andruw Jones for the most postseason RBIs prior to a player’s 23rd birthday. … With his eighth-inning base hit, Contreras became the first Brewers player with 10 hits in this postseason.
Dodgers: Tucker (.304) has consistently swung the bat well through seven games, but he has been the exception to the rule for a cold Dodgers offense. In Game 3, Ohtani (113.5 mph single) and Smith (two-run double) showed some positive signs, but they have been L.A.'s most notable slumping bats this postseason.
Anything else fans might want to know?
•  Orel Hershiser and Mike Scioscia will throw out the ceremonial first pitch and say, "It's time for Dodger baseball!" as part of the pregame ceremonies.
• According to the Elias Sports Bureau, this is the eighth time two teams met in the postseason one year after one swept the other in the previous postseason. The only team to be swept and then win a rematch the following postseason is the 1923 Yankees, who won that year's World Series over the New York Giants in six games.
• Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said it struck him that it’s been 44 years since the Brewers made it to the World Series, and 44 is one of the franchise’s retired numbers for Hall of Famer Hank Aaron. This year marked the 50th anniversary of Aaron’s 755th and final home run, which he hit while playing for the Brewers in 1976.
• This marks the sixth time a team has taken a 3-0 series lead against the reigning World Series champion in a best-of-seven series. Four of the previous five -- 1990 WS, Reds vs A’s; 1966 WS, Orioles vs Dodgers; 1963 WS, Dodgers vs Yankees; 1914 WS, Boston Braves vs Philadelphia Athletics -- ended in a sweep. The other (2017 NLCS, Dodgers vs Cubs) concluded with the Dodgers winning in five games.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles — When dynasties fall, it is not insurrection, nor jealousy, nor sloth that bring them down. It is the undefeated champion of the world, Father Time. We are watching the Los Angeles Dodgers age out.
The Milwaukee Brewers proved for a third time in the National League Championship Series they are the better (and younger) team, completing a beautiful triptych of comebacks with a 6-2 win in Game 3 on Wednesday. In three successive games, the Dodgers had Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Blake Snell on the mound with a lead and lost all three. Ninety-five million dollars, four Cy Young awards and a World Series MVP worth of pitching and they could not hold back Milwaukee any more than you can hold back water with your hands.
But the most obvious reason why the Brewers have put the Dodger dynasty on the brink of extinction is this: the youngest pitching staff in baseball—and the hardest throwing staff in postseason history—has smothered the oldest team in baseball. Milwaukee is pushing around the aging Dodgers lineup with a barrage of fastballs in three versions, especially power sinkers. They are shoving 66.8% fastballs at the Dodgers at an average velocity of 97.9 mph. The Dodgers’ only path to victory is to slug and the Brewers simply won’t allow it.
“I just think they’re really good pitchers,” Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas said. “A lot of their pitchers throw three different fastballs. They throw hard, and they’ve been locating the ball really well. They haven’t really given us too much of an opportunity to kind of build momentum.
“They’ve been attacking the zone. They throw their stuff in the zone—and with all three fastballs. A lot of guys have a cutter, a sinker and a four-seam fastball. It’s really hard to put barrels on the ball.
“At the end of the day, it’s just the velocity of their stuff. They throw the ball really hard. And we all know when you throw that hard, it’s really hard.”
The Brewers knew coming into the series that in today’s game older players don’t hit elite fastballs as well as younger players, and so the matchup was to their liking. But this? Who could have seen this in the NLCS? The Dodgers:
- Have two extra-base hits in 105 plate appearances
- Have been outhomered, 5-0
- Are the first team in franchise history to lose three straight games in one postseason with no home runs and no attempted stolen bases
- Are hitting .228 against fastballs
- Are 2-for-16 with runners in scoring position, part of a 3-for-32 postseason disaster in those spots
This has been the year in which baseball made a sharp turn when it comes to the speed of the game. Younger players thrive. Velocity, and the widespread adoption of the family of three fastballs, changed everything. You need fast-twitch athleticism, youthfulness. You need this generation of players who know velocity as a first language. You need rangy players on defense. The numbers bear out that younger players are the preferred way to go.
Players 30 and younger this year hit .247. Players in the 31-35 year-old demographic hit 10 points worse, .237, their worst showing ever. There was a time when front offices valued those 31-35 players because it seemed to be the peak intersection of experience and physical tools. Front offices were afraid to commit to younger players because of the lack of reps and track records. Those days are over.
The difference on the field in NLCS Game 3 was striking. The Brewers are the fastest team in baseball, as measured by sprint speed. The Dodgers are 24th.
The Brewers started a lineup and a pitcher with an average age of 26.1. They became the first team in history with a second postseason game starting three players 22 and younger: leftfielder Jackson Chourio, shortstop Cooper Pratt and rightfielder Luis Lara. Chourio opened the game with a first-pitch homer. Pratt smacked three hits, stole a base and scored a run. Lara flew around rightfield like a bird of prey, snaring anything that dared enter his airspace.
Watching Chourio, 22, Garrett Mitchell, 28, and Lara, 21, patrol the outfield was like watching an Olympic sprint relay team.
On the other side of the field, the Dodgers, especially their bats, looked old and slow. The average age of their starting 10 was 32.3 years old—more than six years older than Milwaukee’s fearless group. Only two starting Dodgers were in their 20s: centerfielder Andy Pages, 25, and Kyle Tucker, 29, who with his diminished range and baserunning has been trending older than his age.
By starting eight players 31 and older, these Dodgers joined the 2023 Dodgers, who got bounced by the Diamondbacks, as the only teams in the past 19 postseasons to trot out so many starting players that old in a game.
Fittingly, the old team played an outdated style of baseball, one from a generation ago. The ninth-place hitter, Tommy Edman, twice batted after the leadoff runner reached first base. Twice manager Dave Roberts did not ask him to bunt.
“I thought about it, but it’s just, he had a good pitch to hit. Flew out,” Roberts said. “I just didn’t feel giving up an out right there. Early in the game, I wanted Tommy to hit ...
“We haven’t been getting hits with runners in scoring position. To give up an out, to bank on getting a hit with runners in scoring position, I’d rather just try to maybe slug, hit a double.”
Edman was a below average hitter (97 OPS+) with a .385 slug this season.
Roberts and the Dodgers keep waiting for slug to show up at the expense of forfeiting the situational baseball as deployed by the other three remaining teams, the youthful Brewers, Guardians and Rays. The Dodgers still may be waiting Thanksgiving morning.
For instance, the Dodgers were down 1-0 in the sixth when Roberts sent 36-year-old Max Muncy to hit for Pages with runners on first and second and no outs. In that situation, the Brewers are bunting. Milwaukee plays get-em-over, get-em-in ball. The Dodgers? No way. Muncy is a three-true outcome guy. He is not going to bunt. Again, the Dodgers played for slug and got nothing. Muncy struck out. Will Smith, 31, did save the rally with a two-run double. But the Dodgers would go 1-for-12 after that against hard-throwing relievers D.L. Hall and Trevor Megill.
The lineup remained cold. Shohei Ohtani, 32, cannot pull a baseball because of lower-half injuries that won’t allow him to properly turn his hips and get to a firm front side. Freeman, 37, has three extra-base hits since Aug. 31.
“[Our] pitching staff has been great, to be honest,” Rojas said. “It’s really hard to put it into context when you have to pitch and have to play defense with a one run lead every single time. It’s like asking these guys to just throw a perfect inning every single time. It’s not sustainable. So, the blame is on the offense. We all know we could’ve done better, but nothing we can do now.”
How in the world has Milwaukee made Los Angeles look so bad?
“It’s pretty simple,” Muncy said. “We’ve played like [poop]. They’ve played great.”
Occam’s razor (or commode) aside, the one-sided NLCS is bigger than that. It stands as a changing of the guard, recalling the 1964 World Series, when the St. Louis Cardinals, emblematic of the National League embracing Black and Latin American players, ended the dynasty of an aging New York Yankees team, then the second oldest team in baseball. The younger, faster, harder-throwing, more creative team has been, beyond doubt, the better team.
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Blue Jays' Alejandro Kirk Shares Offseason News Amid Trade Chatter
item.dc:creator: Dibyendu Mondal

item.content:encoded:
Alejandro Kirk gave the Toronto Blue Jays a rare bright spot on an offense that struggled all season.
The catcher hit .278 with a .351 on-base percentage and a .415 slugging percentage. Kirk hit 10 home runs, drove in 43 runs and scored 26 times in 79 games. He collected 77 hits, including eight doubles and drew 33 walks against 38 strikeouts.
Injuries limited Kirk to 79 of Toronto’s 162 games. After a long season, Kirk is spending the offseason with his family.
He reposted photos from a Disney World trip on his Instagram story. The trip included his wife, Sofia Castañeda and their daughter, Emilia. The couple welcomed their daughter on Feb. 28, 2023.
Amid that news, what made headlines was trade chatter surrounding him.
Alejandro Kirk Labelled as a Trade Chip
Trade talk about Kirk surfaced Oct. 11. The Blue Bird Territory podcast posted a clip that day on X. The show features The Athletic’s Mitch Bannon, former Blue Jays outfielder Kevin Pillar and former pitcher Ricky Romero.
The post called Kirk “one of Toronto’s most VALUABLE trade chips.” In the clip, Pillar wondered about Kirk’s market value after injuries cost him much of the season. The clip spread online and some fans took it as a trade pitch.
Should Alejandro Kirk Be Traded?
The short answer is absolutely not. Bannon backed that view on X the same day. He wrote that he, Pillar and Romero all agreed Toronto should keep Kirk.
“This clip has gained some misguided traction, so to be clear, Kevin, Ricky and I all agreed the Jays shouldn’t trade Kirk,” he said. “We were more discussing why there’s been trade talk about him. In fact, I said he’s the exact mold of hitter the Jays covet, not a potential trade guy.”
The case against a trade starts with the contract. Toronto signed Kirk to a five-year, $58 million extension in March 2025. The deal covers 2026 through 2030 and averages $11.6 million per year.
Kirk also produces. His 114 wRC+ in 2026 topped his career mark of 111. He posted that mark despite missing more than two months. He walked in 10.5 percent of his plate appearances and struck out in 12.1 percent.
His defense adds to the case. In 2025, Kirk tied for third in MLB in fielding run value, with 21. He led all catchers in blocks above average and finished as a Gold Glove finalist.
Kirk also delivers in October. The two-time All-Star hit five home runs in the 2025 postseason. That ties the most by a catcher in one postseason. One was a go-ahead, three-run homer in World Series Game 3.
Toronto cannot afford to lose a productive bat. The Blue Jays’ offense was one of baseball’s worst this year. Trading a 27-year-old catcher on a long-term deal would deepen that problem.

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies were eliminated from the MLB playoffs by the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card Series.
The Braves won Games 1 and 3, and the Phillies won Game 2.
The Braves have since been eliminated. Four teams remain in the playoffs. The Milwaukee Brewers have a 3-0 lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS, and the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays are tied 1-1 in the ALCS.
During the Championship Series, the Phillies announced news involving shortstop Trea Turner.
Philadelphia Phillies’ Dave Dombrowski Announces Trea Turner News After Early Playoff Exit
ATLANTA, GEORGIA – SEPTEMBER 30: Trea Turner #7 of the Philadelphia Phillies runs the bases during the first inning against the Atlanta Braves in game two of the National League Wild Card Series at Truist Park on September 30, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)
“He did not have a good year. He needs to fix things with his swing. He knows he has to be better at shortstop. I told him that is mandatory. I told him he cannot play shortstop like he did in 2026, going into 2027.”
Dave Dombrowski told him if he plays shortstop like he did in 2026, then he won’t be playing shortstop. Trea will be working with Carlos Mendoza.
Dave says Turner prefers the infield.
Sounds like Turner will be moved from shortstop if it is not going well in spring training
Trea Turner does not think he had a good season. He takes complete accountability. He is already working on his swing.
Turner flew back into town to speak with Dave Dombrowski for a few hours
Looking at Trea Turner
PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA – SEPTEMBER 25: Trea Turner #7 of the Philadelphia Phillies reacts after a strikeout in the fourth inning during a game against the Tampa Bay Rays at Citizens Bank Park on September 25, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images)
Turner arguably had the worst season of his career in 2026.
The shortstop hit .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs and 58 RBI over 157 games. He recorded -17 Defensive Runs Saved and -8 Outs Above Average over 1,343 1/3 innings at shortstop.
PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA – SEPTEMBER 24: Trea Turner #7 of the Philadelphia Phillies looks on during a game against the Milwaukee Brewers at Citizens Bank Park on September 24, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images)
Turner signed an 11-year, $300 million contract with the Phillies in the 2022-23 offseason.
He accumulated 14.4 fWAR in his first three seasons with the Phillies. This year, he posted just 1.1 fWAR.
Turner began his career with the Washington Nationals in 2015.
The Nationals traded Turner to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the 2021 trade deadline. He played for Los Angeles through the 2022 season then signed his deal with Philadelphia.
Throughout his MLB career, Turner has posted 48.4 fWAR. He is a World Series Champion and a three-time All-Star.

item.title: [Sportsnet.ca] Phillies GM says Turner will be moved off shortstop if poor play continues
item.dc:creator: Sportsnet Staff
item.description: After the worst statistical season of his MLB career, Trea Turner drew the ire of his general manager on Thursday. "He needs to fix things with his swing. He knows he has to be better at shortstop. I told him that is mandatory. I told him he cannot play shortstop like he did in 2026, going into 2027.” Turner, 33, posted a career-low minus-0.1 bWAR. He slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs and 58 RBIs. However, his defensive work was far worse. Turner graded out as a minus-nine by Statcast's f
item.content:encoded:
After the worst statistical season of his MLB career, Trea Turner drew the ire of his general manager on Thursday.
"He needs to fix things with his swing. He knows he has to be better at shortstop. I told him that is mandatory. I told him he cannot play shortstop like he did in 2026, going into 2027.”
Turner, 33, posted a career-low minus-0.1 bWAR. He slashed .242/.297/.378 with 19 home runs and 58 RBIs.
However, his defensive work was far worse. Turner graded out as a minus-nine by Statcast's fielding run value and tied for an MLB low with minus-17 defensive runs saved.
Dombrowski added that Turner will start the season at shortstop, but must play well defensively to continue at the position.
If not, the Phillies GM implied that changes will be made.
According to Dombrowski, Turner agreed that he had a bad season, took full accountability, and is already working on his swing.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees would be wasting Cody Bellinger at first base
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Seventeen home runs aren't enough to make everyone happy with a $162.5 million contract. Cody Bellinger's glove deserves a much fairer hearing than his power total, though, especially when the Yankees start moving names around their 2027 lineup. I'd keep him in left field. Making Bellinger part of a first-base reshuffle might solve a daily playing-time headache, but it would also remove him from the position where he provided his clearest advantage this season. Bellinger gave the Yankees real va
item.content:encoded:
Seventeen home runs aren't enough to make everyone happy with a $162.5 million contract. Cody Bellinger's glove deserves a much fairer hearing than his power total, though, especially when the Yankees start moving names around their 2027 lineup.
I'd keep him in left field. Making Bellinger part of a first-base reshuffle might solve a daily playing-time headache, but it would also remove him from the position where he provided his clearest advantage this season.
Bellinger gave the Yankees real value in left
Wednesday's Gold Glove finalist announcement supplies a timely reminder. Bellinger led left fielders with 21 Defensive Runs Saved and finished with six Outs Above Average. Those measures use different methods and shouldn't be added together. Both, however, describe a useful defender rather than an expensive bat the club needs to hide.
The actual assignments matter. Bellinger started 112 games in left and logged 1,008 2/3 innings there. He made one start at first base. Moving him across the diamond would be a meaningful change to how the Yankees used him, not a harmless continuation of the same role.
New York can still want more offense. Bellinger hit .264/.338/.429 with 17 homers and 73 RBI in 132 games. A .767 OPS doesn't settle whether the five-year investment was wise, and a defensive award nomination certainly doesn't settle it either.
There isn't an obvious platoon problem to solve
His season wasn't built on one comfortable matchup. Bellinger had a .755 OPS against left-handed pitching and .775 against right-handers. Neither number makes him indispensable, but they don't suggest a player who needs to be pulled out of the lineup whenever the opposing starter throws with the wrong hand.
0What do you think?Post a comment.
Moving him would create another assignment
First-base flexibility has uses. On a day when Bellinger needs less running, or when another outfielder offers a clear matchup advantage, the occasional move can help. Committing him there for long stretches would be a different decision, because somebody else would have to handle those left-field innings.
I'd want the Yankees to compare the entire defensive arrangement before making that call. How much better is the new first baseman than the existing option? How much weaker does left field become? A more convenient lineup card can still produce a worse team if those costs are ignored.
There are limits to this argument. Defensive estimates vary, Bellinger's future health can't be assumed, and a genuinely superior outfield addition could change the calculation. The Yankees should remain open to those possibilities instead of treating one position as permanently reserved.
For now, the evidence favors leaving his main job alone. Bellinger can improve at the plate without the Yankees sacrificing what he already does well. Their offseason should be about adding strengths, not moving one of the existing ones to a position where it matters less.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rays-Guardians ALCS Game 3 FAQ, lineups (1 ET, TBS/HBO Max)
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Keegan Matheson; Adam Berry
item.description: CLEVELAND -- It’s a new day in the ALCS, as the Rays and Guardians have shifted their matchup back to Cleveland tied up at 1-1. The Rays' 3-1 win in Game 2 shifted this series back into focus after the Guardians pulled off a 7-3 come-from-behind win in the opener.
